title: Packers By The Numbers: Stats from the Week 7 loss to the Lions
summary: As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports. Today we’re looking at the 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 7. Offense The Packers had a nice personnel mix in this game, leaning a bit heavier on 11 […]
full_text: (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports . Today we’re looking at the 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 7. Offense The Packers had a nice personnel mix in this game, leaning a bit heavier on 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) than we’ve seen from some other games, but this feels like their best mix for the team they have. The Packers didn’t have a great day on offense overall, but 11 was their best personnel grouping. It was slightly underperforming in terms of Success Rate (34.9% in 11, 35.7% in 12), but it was their best by EPA (+0.21 EPA per Play). They turned in a +0.37 EPA per Play on passes out of 11 personnel. Jordan Love was under pressure on 37.0% of his dropbacks, which is right in line with the Lions pressure rate on the season (36.7%). The biggest difference is the time to pressure. On the season, the Lions are averaging 2.65 seconds to pressure (16th in the league). In this game, they averaged 2.4 seconds to pressure (which would the second best rate in the league this year, just below the Giants at 2.38 seconds). So this offensive line essentially turned a middle-of-the-road pass rush team into the second best pass rush in the league. The offensive line is functional in a way that it wasn’t in the first couple of weeks, but it certainly is still pretty far below average. For the game, Love averaged 2.61 seconds to throw, which feels like an eternity based on some of the games we’ve seen this season (this marked his 3rd longest time to throw of the season, behind the Cowboys at 2.88 and Bears at 2.67). That 2.61 average would have been the 2nd fastest time to throw among all QBs in the 2025 season (behind Aaron Rodgers at 2.59 seconds and just ahead of Tua Tagovailoa at 2.65 seconds). Despite all that, Love averaged 10.9 ADOT (Average Depth of Target) and an EPA per Play of +0.14. If not for the drops (which I have not yet charted), the EPA per Play and Success Rate numbers would look quite a bit better. Another rough day for the receivers (and running backs) catching the ball. Tough day for play action. The Packers have not been a heavy play action team this year (20.1%, 25th in the league in play action rate), but it has been a solid play for them (+0.32 EPA per Play, 5th in the league). In this game they had a play action rate of 20% and an EPA per Play of -0.64. Again, I need to chart the drops at some point and see how much of an impact those had on some of these numbers. The Packers went with a more pass-heavy attack in this game. They were at a 70.8% pass rate. That’s higher than I think they’d like to be (somewhere in the 65% range seems to be where they’re aiming), but, based on how the run game has gone, I don’t mind a 70% pass rate. That pass rate was pretty consistent by down. Here are their pass rates by down in this game: 1st: 66.7% 2nd: 76.5% 3rd: 70% 4th: 70.6% Their 1st down passing EPA was their best down of the day (+0.825 EPA per Play, 57.1% Success Rate). The return of Josh Jacobs was…fine? He finished with 36 yards on 11 attempts, with 30 of those yards coming after contact. Here are his numbers by defensive box count: He looked better than what the Packers have had so far, but not massively so. His stuff as a receiver looked a bit better. He had 5 catches (on 7 targets) for 55 yards (+1.25 EPA per Reception). His Average Depth of Target of 5.1 yards means he was being targeted downfield. In fact, he currently stands as the only Packers running back who has been targeted past the line of scrimmage. Here are the ADOT numbers for the other Packers running backs: Kaleb Johnson: -0.33 MarShawn Lloyd: -0.69 Pierre Strong: -0.7 Chris Brooks: -1.4 The running game may not be transformed, but if they’re willing to target the running backs more on vertical routes, I’ll take it. (But also catch the passes that hit you in the hands in the end zone.) MarShawn Lloyd turning in his best EPA on runs outside the tackle feels pretty on brand… …but also he looked better this week than he had. A little more decisive. Some strong finishes. He may never turn into anything, but I thought there was a bit of promise this week. Or maybe that’s pure hope. Defense The Lions went heavy personnel in this game: That led to the Packers leaning more into Base Personnel than we’ve seen over the past few weeks. They were in Nickel more they have shown this season based on the heavier personnel usage, but I don’t know if that’s because that’s what they wanted to do or if the injury to Zaire Franklin changed their approach. Personally, I don’t mind leaning more on Nickel. I don’t really love any scenario that leads to Javon Bullard being taken off the field. Not a great day for the pass rush group. They blitzed 30.3% of the time but only pressured Goff on 24.2% of dropbacks (15.1% below the NFL average). Gannon has done a nice job of creating a pass rush this season (and some nice individual efforts have popped up), but this is the first game where I truly felt the loss of Micah Parsons. They did some nice work against the run (their 18.2% Tackle For Loss Rate was 7.1% above the NFL Average), but Goff felt comfortable for the vast majority of the day. Albums listened to: Michael Kiwanuka – FUDGE

title: Packers Snap Counts Week 7: Who was on the field vs. the Lions?
summary: There were a lot of moving parts on the Green Bay Packers’ roster coming into the week, as the team made four moves on Saturday to piece together a roster to play the Detroit Lions. There were also three in-game injuries for the Packers, on top of Green Bay missing starting Mike linebacker Zaire Franklin. […]
full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images There were a lot of moving parts on the Green Bay Packers’ roster coming into the week, as the team made four moves on Saturday to piece together a roster to play the Detroit Lions. There were also three in-game injuries for the Packers, on top of Green Bay missing starting Mike linebacker Zaire Franklin. With all that chaos swirling around, who was on the field for the Packers on Sunday? Let’s go position-by-position to explain what is changing on this team, and what to expect from the personnel moving forward. Quarterback Jordan Love: 65 snaps Tyrod Taylor: 0 Running Back Josh Jacobs: 35 MarShawn Lloyd: 22 Pierre Strong Jr.: 8 Scratch: Kaleb Johnson Running back Josh Jacobs returned to the Packers as a full-time starter for the team, playing 54 percent of Green Bay’s overall offensive snaps in Week 7. For perspective, he played 59 percent of the Packers’ offensive snaps in the 15 games that he suited up for last season. For the most part, he played his full share of reps, instead of being on a pitch count. The players who were pushed down by Jacobs’ addition were Pierre Strong Jr., who is now clearly the RB3 in Green Bay, and Kaleb Johnson, who is now a healthy scratch for the Packers. It will be interesting to see what Green Bay will do whenever Chris Brooks, who split time with Lloyd until Brooks’ injury, is activated from the injured reserve. I wouldn’t be shocked if Brooks takes Strong’s place on the 53-man roster, and the Packers try to re-sign Strong to the practice squad. There’s value in Johnson’s rookie contract, which would terminate if they waive him, as he’s still on a three-year cost-controlled deal. Receiver Matthew G0lden: 55 Christian Watson: 53 Savion Williams: 40 Bo Melton: 13 J. Michael Sturdivant: 4 Coleman Owen: 0 It’s clear at this point that Savion Williams is the Packers’ answer for losing Jayden Reed and Skyy Moore at the slot position. He’s been getting premier looks as Green Bay’s WR3, over Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant. Coleman Owen has played two weeks without an offensive snap, as he’s been limited to the punt returner position. Melton is the Packers’ kick returner, with Sturdivant playing as the “off returner.” Previously, Moore was the team’s punt and kick returner, with Melton as the “off returner.” Tight End Tucker Kraft: 57 Mark Redman: 16 Jonnu Smith: 15 Josh Whyle: 7 Outside of one odd week, the Packers’ TE4 has been Josh Whyle this entire season. Mark Redman and Jonnu Smith are generally the team’s TE2 and TE3, but they play different roles. Redman usually comes in for more blocking situations, while Smith comes in for more route-running situations. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 65 Laken Tomlinson: 65 Travis Glover: 65 Anthony Belton: 65 John Williams: 56 Jacob Monk: 5 Sean Rhyan: 4 Aaron Banks: 0 Scratch: Kevin Zeitler, Donovan Jennings and Jager Burton The Packers only got nine combined snaps out of their top center (Sean Rhyan) and top backup at the position (Jacob Monk) before they both exited the game with injuries and never returned. Head coach Matt LaFleur has already said that they will both miss action against the Carolina Panthers next week on Thursday Night Football , so assume that John Williams will make his first career start in Week 8. The only good news here is that Green Bay is oversigned at the offensive line position, so it’ll be easy for the team to slide in players with experience for those injuries. I think the Packers will have a bench of Aaron Banks, Kevin Zeitler and Donovan Jennings next week. Jennings will probably be the “next man up” at center, with Banks and/or Zeitler “next man up” at guard. If there’s an injury at tackle, we’re probably going to see Travis Glover have to slide out from right guard. Defensive Line Karl Brooks: 46 Chris McClellan: 38 Jordon Riley: 29 Anthony Campbell: 26 Devonte Wyatt: 23 Devonte Wyatt left this game early with an injury before coming back, which opened up a lot of snaps for Jordon Riley in the second half, right off an activation from the PUP list — where he started the year recovering from his season-ending Achilles injury. This was the second-half snap count for the interior defensive linemen: Brooks: 25 McClellan: 25 Riley: 21 Campbell: 16 Wyatt: 11 This is also a huge jump in snaps for McClellan, who was behind Brooks, Wyatt, Javon Hargrave (IR) and Jonathan Ford (IR) to start the year (with Warren Brinson also ahead of him until his preseason injury). Quickly, the rookie third-round pick has gone from DL6 to DL2 in the pecking order, due to injury. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness: 41 Dani Dennis-Sutton: 33 Barryn Sorrell: 32 Brenton Cox Jr.: 28 Arron Mosby: 0 The Packers continue to rotate their edge defender room liberally, and the Lions didn’t pass all that much when Lukas Van Ness was on the field. Between the runs the team saw with Van Ness on the grass, plus the fact that Van Ness dropped into coverage a few times when blitzers came from elsewhere, Van Ness only rushed the passer 15 total times against Detroit. So more than half of the time Lions quarterback Jared Goff was dropping back, Van Ness wasn’t coming after him. Off-Ball Linebacker Isaiah McDuffie: 66 Ty’Ron Hopper: 62 Nick Niemann: 1 Kristian Welch: 0 Scratch: Zaire Franklin (injury) With Zaire Franklin out with a shin injury, it was expected that Isaiah McDuffie would start at the Mike spot and Ty’Ron Hopper would start at the Will spot. That’s exactly what we got tonight. Hopefully, Franklin can play against the Panthers, as the Packers’ blitzes from the linebacker position didn’t go anywhere against the Lions, and Goff picked apart Green Bay’s zone defense over the middle of the field. Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 65 Brandon Cisse: 65 Carrington Valentine: 4 Kamal Hadden: 0 Scratch: Benjamin St-Juste (injury) Nothing new here. Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse are the starters, and Carrington Valentine is playing a couple of dime snaps here and there as the second slot defender. Safety Xavier McKinney: 66 Evan Williams: 66 Javon Bullard: 35 Kitan Oladapo: 0 The Lions played a lot more heavy sets on offense, as we expected . Because of that, slot defender Javon Bullard was only on the field for 53 percent of the snaps on defense this week. Against Dallas the week before, which played a lot more three-receiver looks, Bullard played 86 percent of the time.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: NFC Playoff Picture: Green Bay Packers are still in position despite loss
summary: The Green Bay Packers are last in the NFC North. That is true. But they are in the only division in the NFC where all the teams are over .500 and they still hold a playoff spot despite losing to the Detroit Lions on Sunday. The Minnesota Vikings are the lone undefeated team in the […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Jameson Williams #1 of the Detroit Lions runs the ball against against the Green Bay Packers during the first quarter at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are last in the NFC North. That is true. But they are in the only division in the NFC where all the teams are over .500 and they still hold a playoff spot despite losing to the Detroit Lions on Sunday. The Minnesota Vikings are the lone undefeated team in the NFC following the loss by the San Francisco 49ers. The Chicago Bears won on Thursday. And you already know about the Detroit Lions beating the Packers. So the NFC North had a great week outside of one team, and all of them are in a playoff spot heading into Week 8. title: LaFleur: Trey Smack is the Packers’ kicker; 2 OL expected to be out on TNF
summary: In his post-game press conference on Sunday after the Green Bay Packers’ last-second loss to the Detroit Lions, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said Trey Smack will be Green Bay’s kicker moving forward, so don’t expect the team to move off the rookie this week. As a reminder, the Packers play their second Thursday Night Football game […]
full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images In his post-game press conference on Sunday after the Green Bay Packers’ last-second loss to the Detroit Lions, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said Trey Smack will be Green Bay’s kicker moving forward, so don’t expect the team to move off the rookie this week. As a reminder, the Packers play their second Thursday Night Football game of the season next week, this time against the Carolina Panthers, so the green and gold will have another abbreviated week of practice. Smack missed two field goals of under 35 yards, making him the first kicker in the entire NFL season to do so, in the loss against Detroit. One of those kicks was blocked. As a rookie, Smack is now 11 of 16 on field goals, with four misses coming over the last three weeks. Smack has also missed two extra points in 2026. Beyond the Smack news, LaFleur also stated that it’s his expectation that both Sean Rhyan and Jacob Monk, the two centers who went down with injuries early on in Week 7’s action, will miss next week’s game against Carolina. He wouldn’t comment on whether those injuries are expected to be long-term issues, but right now it looks like John Williams, who got his first offensive NFL snaps on Sunday, will be the team’s center verus the Panthers. Green Bay came into the week “oversigned” on the offensive line, which forced them to make three scratches on the position to make a 48-man game-day roster. More than likely, the team will not make a move on the offensive line, but will instead activate two of Kevin Zeitler, Donovan Jennings and Jager Burton, the three offensive linemen they scratched in Week 7. Two of those players, along with Aaron Banks, should be the Packers’ backups on the line next week.

title: Packers vs. Lions Final Score: Green Bay squanders chances in 20-17 loss
summary: It’s tough to win a football game when you’re not only competing against an opposing team, but also the referees. Yet again, officiating has become a major talking point for the Green Bay Packers. On Sunday afternoon in Detroit, the Packers were flagged multiple times in the second half, drawing inexplicable penalties that whole seeing […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers runs the ball for a first down against the Detroit Lions during the first quarter at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s tough to win a football game when you’re not only competing against an opposing team, but also the referees. Yet again, officiating has become a major talking point for the Green Bay Packers. On Sunday afternoon in Detroit, the Packers were flagged multiple times in the second half, drawing inexplicable penalties that whole seeing similar – or more egregious – conduct by the Detroit Lions go uncalled. Meanwhile, rookie kicker Trey Smack continued his struggles, missing twice from inside 40 yards to keep six points that they should have scored off the board. One of the most meaningful penalties of the game came at the two minute warning, however, as Karl Brooks jumped offsides in a tie game to give Detroit a first down. That gave the Lions just enough of a chance to run clock off for a last second game winning field goal, which Jake Bates hit to give the Lions the win. The Packers started the game with the football and Matt LaFleur showed an aggressive nature early on the drive. Jordan Love came out slinging to Matthew Golden, who had two receptions for 27 yards on the drive. LaFleur kept his offense on the field on a 4th-and-5 from the Lions’ 33 and Love delivered a strike to Savion Williams for 27 yards of his own. But after that, he went back to the run game behind Josh Jacobs, running twice for three yards to set up a 3rd-and-goal at the 3. Love got flushed from the pocket and threw incomplete to Golden, but Trey Smack missed a chip shot wide right, ending a promising first drive with zero points. Detroit made the Packers pay for their missed opportunity quickly. Jared Goff led a six-play, 80-yard touchdown drive, finishing it off with consecutive passes to Jameson Williams, first for 24 yards and then for a 16-yard score as the Lions took an early 7-0 lead. The Packers went for another short 4th down on their next drive, this time a 4th-and-2 from midfield. Love hit a wide-open Tucker Kraft for 22 yards. Kraft finished the job this time, as Love rolled out and found him in the right corner of the end zone for a 14-yard score ON NATIONAL TIGHT ENDS DAY 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/hYRT7RjpE0 — Green Bay Packers (@packers) October 25, 2026 The tie game was short-lived, thanks to a 40-yard pass from Goff to Amon-Ra St. Brown, but the Packers got a pair of tackles for loss in their own territory to force a field goal from Jake Bates. That gave the Lions a 10-7 lead, and they had a chance to extend it after a three-and-out by Green Bay on their next series. However, Jonathan Gannon’s defense returned the favor, getting off the field quickly for the first time all game. Savion Williams delivered another big catch to move the chains on the Packers’ next drive, hauling in a 20-yard gain on 3rd-and-9 on the opening set of downs. Yet another 4th down attempt resulted in a big play, this time with Love hooking up with Christian Watson for a 28-yard gain to reach the red zone. The first failed 4th down attempt of the game came three plays later, however, as the Packers came up empty once again. The Lions drove down the field late in the first half and looked to be threatening to convert on the first half of a double-up around the halftime break, but a lucky break kept them off the scoreboard. Detroit ran 12 plays and picked up 85 yards on the drive, but Isaiah McDuffie recovered a Jahmyr Gibbs fumble — which appeared to be caused by Lions center Cade Mays — giving the Packers the game’s first takeaway and sending them into the half with just a three-point deficit. Coming out of the half, the Packers’ defense did it again. Mays had a bad exchange with Goff and McDuffie fell on the football a second time, setting Green Bay up in great field position with a chance to take the lead back. They did just that, as Josh Jacobs made his first truly big play of the game and the season. On 3rd-and-6, Love found Jacobs with a dump-off, and he broke multiple tackles, tight-roping his way up the sideline and into the end zone for a 25-yard touchdown. Oh my goodness! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/JxepR2jP24 — Green Bay Packers (@packers) October 25, 2026 Trey Smack’s PAT put the Packers up 14-10, giving Green Bay their first lead of the game, but it would be short-lived. Jameson Williams had a 30-yard reception to get the drive across midfield then got open over the middle for a 10-yard touchdown, his second of the game, to push the Lions back in front once again. After yet another stalled Packers drive, the defense had to come up with yet another clutch stop despite several flags on the defense – most egregious of them being an awful roughing the passer on Brenton Cox that wiped out a third down stop. But after Brandon Cisse’s interception was erased by a pass interference call on him in the red zone, the rookie came up with a pass breakup in the end zone on 4th-and-5 to turn the ball over on downs. More bad calls (and no-calls) hurt the Packers’ offense as the fourth quarter began. Love was flagged for intentional grounding despite clearly trying to throw the ball to Tucker Kraft – Jared Goff was not flagged for a nearly identical play earlier in the game – and an eventual deep ball on 3rd and long got picked off by Brian Branch. Evan Williams got his hands on two passes on the Lions’ next drive. He was unable to haul either one in, but they did help force a 3-and-out once again. The Packers managed to tie the game on their next drive, getting some big plays from Josh Jacobs and drawing an unnecessary roughness penalty on a Lions defender. Smack eventually hit from 43 yards out, knotting the score at 17. Dan Campbell’s aggressive nature came back to burn him deep in Detroit’s own territory on the ensuing series. Facing a 4th-and-2 from inside their own 30, the he called a run to Gibbs but Keisean Nixon read the play perfectly and wrapped up the back in the backfield. The Lions caught a huge break, as the Packers failed to score. Josh Jacobs dropped a would-be touchdown pass and Trey Smack missed again, this time from 35 yards out. Smack’s kick appeared to be tipped ever so slightly by DJ Wonnum, but it still goes down as a miss in crunch time. Yet another horrendous roughing the passer call went against Green Bay as the Lions quickly moved across midfield, looking for a go ahead score. Even Tom Brady, on the call for FOX, was baffled by the call against Karl Brooks, and officiating analyst Dean Blandino called the hit “teaching tape.” But a flag it remained, setting Detroit up to run off more clock before facing a 3rd-and-5 at the Packers’ 20 after the 2 minute warning. Brooks made a dreadful and legitimate mistake, however, jumping offside and giving Detroit a first down and a chance to run off most of the remaining clock with Green Bay having just one timeout left. Gibbs picked up one last first down to run the clock out and give Jake Bates an easy game-winning field goal.

full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 25: Cade Stover #8 of the Houston Texans celebrates a two point conversion with Ed Ingram #69 of the Houston Texans during the second quarter against the New York Giants at NRG Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are seven games into the season and we are still stuck with the central question when it comes to the Houston Texans: what exactly are you? Are they a passing team that gives up fourteen penalties a game (like they did today, of which 10 were accepted)? Are they a smashmouth team with a defense that can stop anybody (except in overtime when they got absolutely steamrolled by Cam Skattebo and the Giants)? Are they good? Are they bad? Well, today’s 27-21 loss to the New York Giants, those last two questions feel pretty irrelevant. They are what they are and boy are they ever that. Texans played down to their opponents yet again, racking up 237 yards of total offense a touchdown pass to Marvin Harrison Jr. (his first with the Texans) and an Xavier Hutchinson rush are the only touchdowns the Texans could get. And the defense simply had no answers for J.J. McCarthy and Cam Skattebo. I want you to read that statement again. The Houston Texans defense had no answers for a pretty pedestrian Giants offense; which they allowed to score 27 points and 420 yards of total offense. But most of all, we need to talk about Kamari Lassiter. Something is clearly wrong and his play has suffered as a result. Also, too, the defense is weak against explosive plays now. That’s fun. At any rate, this week is over, possibly the season, and the Texans go into their off week with way more questions in front of them than a Super Bowl caliber team should encounter at this point of the season.

title: Colts should be sellers, but which stars should they actually move?
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are approaching a crossroads, and with the NFL trade deadline quickly approaching, the organization has some difficult decisions to make. Chris Ballard’s dismissal signaled that ownership is no longer satisfied with the direction of the franchise, and Sunday’s 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings only reinforced how far this team remains from […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates during the third quarter of the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are approaching a crossroads, and with the NFL trade deadline quickly approaching, the organization has some difficult decisions to make. Chris Ballard’s dismissal signaled that ownership is no longer satisfied with the direction of the franchise, and Sunday’s 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings only reinforced how far this team remains from competing with the NFL’s best. At 2-5, the Colts have lost three consecutive games, and their playoff hopes are looking increasingly bleak. Over the past week, I examined the hypothetical trade value of three of Indianapolis’ biggest stars: Jonathan Taylor , DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson . Those articles focused on what each player could realistically command on the trade market, without necessarily arguing that the Colts should move any of them. Given the team’s deteriorating situation, however, it is worth taking that discussion one step further. I believe Indianapolis should approach the deadline as a seller, although there is an important distinction between selling valuable assets and conducting a complete fire sale. The Colts still have talented players worth building around, and trading every established veteran for draft capital would risk creating even more problems for whoever takes over as general manager. The objective should be to identify players whose value to a contender is greater than their value to Indianapolis over the next couple of seasons, while retaining those who could play important roles in the next competitive window. That brings us to five players worth discussing, beginning with three veterans whose contracts expire after this season. DeForest Buckner — Trade Of the five players on this list, Buckner is the one I would be most comfortable moving before the deadline. This has very little to do with his performance. Buckner is still one of the best defensive players on the Colts, remains a productive interior pass rusher and has shown few signs of a significant decline at 32 years old. However, his contract expires after this season, and with Indianapolis potentially entering another transitional period, there is a legitimate question about whether keeping him for another few months accomplishes anything meaningful. Buckner has also appeared increasingly frustrated with the state of the franchise in his recent interviews, and it is difficult to blame him. He has spent the past six-plus seasons in Indianapolis, endured multiple quarterback changes and coaching uncertainties, and has yet to experience the sustained success the organization envisioned when it acquired him from San Francisco. At this stage of his career, an opportunity to join a legitimate contender might be mutually beneficial. #Colts DT DeForest Buckner, asked his level of frustration: “I don’t know. How about you guess. Yeah, I’m frustrated. Same thing, we lost.” Where do the Colts go from here and how does he stay sane? “Couldn’t tell you.” What’s missing? “I don’t know. … I couldn’t tell you.” pic.twitter.com/BDlUyXJLi3 — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) October 25, 2026 There is also an interesting development along the Colts’ defensive line that makes moving Buckner considerably easier to justify. Adetomiwa Adebawore is beginning to emerge as a legitimate interior pass-rushing threat. The former fourth-round pick has shown considerable improvement this season, including an impressive two-sack performance against Minnesota on Sunday. He has the athleticism and explosiveness to create problems from the interior and could potentially develop into Buckner’s long-term replacement. That does not mean Adebawore is already as good as Buckner, but giving him a larger role over the remainder of the season would provide Indianapolis with a much clearer understanding of what it has in the young defensive lineman. If the Colts are serious about transitioning toward a younger roster, creating opportunities for players like Adebawore should be part of the process. In my previous article, I projected Buckner’s trade value at a 2027 fourth-round pick. Given his age and expiring contract, that remains a reasonable expectation, and I believe Indianapolis should accept such an offer without much hesitation. The Colts could potentially receive compensatory draft capital if Buckner leaves in free agency, but that is far from guaranteed. He could sign a shorter, team-friendly contract with a contender, Indianapolis could offset his departure through its own free-agent signings, or he could even decide to retire. Any compensatory selection would also arrive in 2028. A guaranteed fourth-round pick in 2027, combined with an opportunity to evaluate Adebawore in a larger role, makes too much sense to ignore. Grover Stewart — Keep Stewart presents a much more complicated situation, even though his age and contract are similar to Buckner’s. At 33 years old, Stewart is playing out the final season of his three-year, $39 million contract and is unlikely to attract significant interest beyond teams looking for an established run-stuffing defensive tackle. His value comes primarily from his ability to occupy blockers, control the line of scrimmage and create opportunities for the linebackers playing behind him. That role is important, but it is also relatively specialized. Teams are generally less willing to surrender meaningful draft capital for a veteran defensive tackle whose primary responsibility is stopping the run rather than generating pressure on opposing quarterbacks. I would estimate Stewart’s trade value at approximately a fifth-round pick, with a fourth-round selection representing a particularly strong return. The problem is that losing Stewart would create a much bigger hole in the Colts’ defense than that compensation suggests. Jerry Tillery is currently the primary alternative at nose tackle, and he represents a substantial downgrade from Stewart, particularly against the run. Indianapolis also has a linebacker group that has struggled with consistency, making Stewart’s ability to occupy interior blockers even more important. Removing him would place additional pressure on a defensive front that has already experienced plenty of difficulties this season. There is also something to be said for retaining a veteran who continues to contribute in several areas. Stewart’s blocked field goal against Minnesota on Sunday was another reminder of the impact he can provide beyond traditional defensive statistics. Unlike Buckner, whose departure could open the door for an emerging player at the same position, trading Stewart would leave Indianapolis without an obvious replacement. The Colts would almost certainly have to address nose tackle during the offseason, potentially using some of the draft capital acquired in the trade just to find someone capable of filling the role. If another team offered a surprisingly strong package, I would certainly listen. However, moving Stewart for a fifth-round pick accomplishes relatively little, especially when Indianapolis could explore bringing him back on a more affordable contract next season. For now, I would keep him. Quenton Nelson — Keep, unless the offer is too good Nelson might be the most difficult decision of the entire group. At 30 years old, he remains one of the NFL’s best guards and has arguably been the Colts’ most consistently dominant player since arriving in Indianapolis in 2018. His contract expires after this season, but unlike some of the other veterans on this list, there is little indication that Nelson is particularly eager to leave the organization. Quenton Nelson, 30, is in a contract year. He was asked today about wanting to be with the #Colts long term:…

The Colts are currently heavy underdogs at +7.5 points. The money line is +330 while the over/under comes in at 46.5. This is the kind of loss that stays with you for a bit because the Colts had chances to win. Going to Minnesota and playing that defense was always going to be tough. Going up seven early was the best recipe as the running game produced for most of the afternoon. The defense hung tough and kept the Colts in the game. Two misses from the reliable Spencer Shrader hang heavy over this one as the Colts dropped another opportunity. This is the second week in a row that the Colts are catching a team coming off their bye. The Jaguars lost to the Texans at home last week in a back and forth affair. Trevor Lawrence topped 300 yards and put four touchdowns on the board, but it wasn’t enough. After tying the game late in the fourth, the Texans marched down the field and kicked the game-winner. Jacksonville has two weeks to think about that and will look to take it out on the Colts. It’s do or die for the Colts. Another loss could trigger a fire sale and mark the end of the season, halfway through the year. The Jaguars are looking to further create distance in the division and start to pull away. The last place the Colts want to play is somewhere they must walk away with a win. It’s going to take everything they have.

full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Minnesota Vikings defensive end Dallas Turner #15 and safety Harrison Smith #22 sack Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones #17 in the second quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium — October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images An inspired defensive effort gave the offense every opportunity to leave Minnesota with a victory Sunday, but an absent passing attack, two rare missed field goals and another deciding turnover delivered a familiar defeat. The Indianapolis Colts lost 16-10 to the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium, dropping their third straight game and falling to 2-5 this season. Indianapolis led 10-6 at halftime, but could not engineer any points in the second half. It felt like another cruel reminder of how badly it has unraveled as the Colts have earned as many wins overseas between Berlin and London as they have stateside over the past calendar year. Daniel Jones finished 13 of 22 for just 108 passing yards, throwing his seventh decisive interception to end the final drive. The Colts entered Sunday with a minus-8 turnover margin, which was the worst in the NFL. Minnesota averaged a league-high two takeaways per game, and Indianapolis lost the turnover battle again, on the final chance to win the game. The defense did enough to win and star running back Jonathan Taylor showcased he can still generate the most explosive play of the game. But when the offense scores just 10 points, the glaring mistakes and missed field goals cost the Colts another game. The Colts did not need perfection Sunday, but they needed their offense to finish drives. Perhaps the biggest issue with backup QB Anthony Richardson Sr. was his inability to sustain drives, but it’s near malpractice to not consider a change or at least include a package for the dual-threat QB to play snaps inside the red zone. Unbelievable. Shane Steichen says he has not considered a QB change because he believes in Daniel Jones. Why? #Colts #ForTheShoe #Vikings #INDvsMIN pic.twitter.com/1NyiTB9VNL — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) October 25, 2026 Jaylahn Tuimoloau and Akeem Davis-Gaither stuffed Vikings running back Aaron Jones in the backfield on fourth down to force a turnover on downs on their opening drive. Indianapolis broke the ice as Daniel Jones relied on his security blanket to move the chains. Facing third down, Jones hit receiver Keenan Allen on a slant to move the sticks near midfield. Three plays later, Jones motioned Josh Downs across the formation and found his slot receiver on a hitch to convert another third down. Taylor took over from there with the longest play from scrimmage, breaking through the Vikings touted defense for a 38-yard touchdown run to give Indianapolis an early 7-0 lead. Taylor led the Colts with 110 scrimmage yards, including 95 rushing yards on 18 carries and one touchdown. Jonathan Taylor breaks through! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/lcFr4An7JV — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 25, 2026 The defense had opportunities to get stops as Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell was aggressive with two early tries on fourth down. Quarterback Kyler Murray moved the Vikings into Colts territory four times in the first half, but Indianapolis forced Minnesota to settle for a pair of field goals as Will Reichard connected from 28 and 47-yards out on consecutive drives to cut the deficit to 7-6. Aside from the missed opportunities on special teams, the two most costly sequences for the Colts were clearly the end of each half. Indianapolis appeared poised to extend its lead with the offense set up seven yards from the end zone with goal-to-go inside the final minute of the first half. An offensive holding penalty pushed the Colts backward, then Jones took an inexcusable 11-yard sack on second down that let the game clock wind down. Spencer Shrader salvaged the 22-play drive with a 43-yard field goal as time expired to give the Colts a 10-6 lead at halftime. The second half was a much different story for Shrader. He missed wide left on a tough 56-yarder that wasted a 13-play drive, then missed a 48-yarder wide right that squandered a chance to level the score late in the final frame. Minnesota’s relentless pass rush overwhelmed Indianapolis, gathering consecutive sacks to force a punt that flipped field position. Shrader’s first miss proved costly after the first play of the fourth quarter when Murray opened with a 35-yard scramble. Murray found tight end T.J. Hockenson near the pylon for a 5-yard touchdown to take a 13-10 lead. The Colts answered with another four-minute drive into Vikings territory, only to settle for a chance to tie and watched Shrader miss a 48-yard field goal wide right with just 4:22 left to play. When the league-leading scorer leaves six points on the field, it was no secret that this game was slipping out of reach. To give credit where it’s due, Indianapolis refused to fold as defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore delivered a breakout performance with five tackles and two sacks, including a key takedown of Murray late in the fourth. Needing a stop to stay within striking distance, cornerback Kenneth Harris also stepped up and broke up a pass to force Reichard to settle for a 52-yard field goal with 1:39 remaining. Tomi does it again 💥 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/5Lvz0Q3UiG — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 25, 2026 The Colts still had one final chance to drive down the field against a Minnesota defense that had not allowed a fourth-quarter touchdown all season. Jones opened the final possession with a 15-yard completion to Downs, giving Indianapolis a lifeline. Then Jones lofted his second pass over the middle, where veteran safety Harrison Smith was waiting to jump the route and picked it off, terminating the final drive and sealing Minnesota’s sixth-straight victory. The rivalry win over Houston offered a brief reprieve, but Indianapolis is still searching for answers after a change in the front office. With three straight losses and the lack of consistency on either side of the ball, the pressure on coach Shane Steichen only intensified. Indianapolis needs its kicker to deliver in the clutch and its franchise quarterback to make a play when the game is on the line, but right now, even that seems like just too much to ask for an organization on the cusp of a fire sale.

full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 18: Indianapolis Colts Mascot Blue in the tunnel prior to the start of and NFL game between the Tennessee Titans and the Indianapolis Colts on October 18, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium at Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are on the road to take on the Minnesota Vikings for week 7 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. Well ladies and gentlemen, today is the first game in the post Chris Ballard era. The game that ended Ballard’s tenure was a 26-20 loss to a previously winless Titans team, a team that has often looked like the worst team in the league so far this season. After that loss, someone had to go and Carlie Irsay-Gordon knew it. She let Chris Ballard know he would need to update his resume and released a statement thanking him for his effort. It’s tough to say how the firing will impact the Colts play for the rest of the season but it would be hard to imagine a loss worse than what we saw in week six. Sure, games could be more lopsided, but with a chance to pull to an even 3-3 record, still solidly in the hunt for the AFC South, Indy (more or less) at full strength, lost to the worst team in the NFL. It actually can’t get much worse. Side Note: I told you about this last week but I’m probably going to keep reminding you each week because I think it’s important for everyone who enjoys these gameday threads. The SB Nation app makes commenting, especially in these game feeds, so much easier. At this point I roll my eyes every time someone asks me to download another app, but this one really does improve the experience so much that even I am telling you that if you like to hang out here, chat, celebrate, commiserate, and argue in the comments, this app is actually worth your time. Links are directly below. Join Stampede Blue on game day! Stay on top of every Colts update and debate every snap with other diehard fans. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . The question of who comes out on top today comes down to a couple of factors. Offensively the Vikings are averaging 283 yards and 22 points per game. The Colts are averaging 311 yards and 24 points per game. Neither team is great offensively but Indy has been slightly better. The disparity between the teams comes on defense. The Colts are giving up 351 yards and 27 points per game, while the Vikings are giving up 260 yards and 13 points per. Indy has also turned the ball over 11 times while their defense has just 3 take aways on the year. The Vikings are almost completely opposite, having just 4 turnovers while their defense has forced 10. As far as matchups go, this one could be worse! The Vikings could have an explosive offense going up against this Indy defense, but they don’t. This Indy defense has the amazing ability to make even bad offenses look competent, so the Minnesota offense might look explosive today, after all. Defensively the Vikings might be in for a banner day against a turnover prone Colts offense featuring a QB who has thrown 4 touchdowns to 6 interceptions. In short, this matchup is rough on paper. There is the chance that we do see a bump in play this week, every year teams that make a big firing play a great game directly following that major firing. One criticism of the Ballard Colts has long been that they play to their competition. In a game like this one, that’s probably a good thing, the Vikings are the better team. Today they play an undefeated opponent, we’ll see if they rise to the occasion or if the will of this team is completely broken. If this game goes the way I think it’s going to go, there’s a non-zero chance we see a certain backup quarterback get some snaps in the second half. Prediction: Vikings: 26 Colts: 13 As always, go Colts. RELATED Where to Watch Week Seven This is your week seven open thread so hang out here, chat, celebrate, commiserate, and argue in the comments! Go wild (within reason)! Go Colts!

The story of their season is their slow starts and the decline in play of quarterback Bo Nix compared to the 2025 season. title: Andy Reid on Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker: ‘He’s off a bit’
summary: Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker had multiple big chances to come through against the Seattle Seahawks, as he has done many times in his 10-year career. The first came before halftime, when a long interception return by cornerback Nohl Williams provided a last-second effort to score points before the break. Butker’s 58-yard attempt was […]
full_text: (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker had multiple big chances to come through against the Seattle Seahawks , as he has done many times in his 10-year career. The first came before halftime, when a long interception return by cornerback Nohl Williams provided a last-second effort to score points before the break. Butker’s 58-yard attempt was right down the middle but fell well short. That kept the score at 10-0, instead of a one-score game at halftime. Butker got a second chance to bring the game within one possession later in the contest, with under eight minutes to go. The 45-yard field goal sailed wide right, and the typically clutch kicker helped put Kansas City in an insurmountable hole in their first loss of the season. Obviously, all three phases contributed to the loss, as head coach Andy Reid made clear during his opening remarks at the podium following the game. When asked further about Butker, Reid acknowledged that the three-time Super Bowl champion kicker needs to improve. “He’s been one of the most consistent kickers in football,” Reid started. “He’s off a bit, so gotta fix it.” Butker’s most consistent skill for most of his career has been dialing in long-range kicks. In 2023, he made all five of his regular-season attempts over 50 yards. However, this season, he has made only one of his five such attempts. Harrison Butker's 15 missed kicks (10 FGs, 5 PATs) since start of last season are the most in NFL. — Josh Dubow (@JoshDubowAP) October 26, 2026 It was a talking point last season because of injury concerns for Butker, who had missed time during the 2024 season. However, all signs pointed to Butker being healthy throughout the offseason and into the game schedule. If Butker can’t fault an injury, the 31-year-old may not be the player he used to be, and Kansas City can’t overextend loyalty this season. If Butker doesn’t sharpen his skills before the games get more crucial, the Chiefs should feel justified in bringing in competition for the kicker position. It wasn’t that long ago that Spencer Shrader and Matthew Wright were coming off the street and making game-winners for Kansas City.

title: Chiefs-Seahawks: 4 instant takeaways from deflating loss in Seattle
summary: On Sunday evening, the Kansas City Chiefs lost their first game of the season 20-3 to the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Here are four rapidly written takeaways from the game: 1. Patrick Mahomes feels the backup offensive tackles Quarterback Patrick Mahomes looked uncomfortable from the pocket against the Seahawks, and it’s a reminder […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday evening, the Kansas City Chiefs lost their first game of the season 20-3 to the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks . Here are four rapidly written takeaways from the game: 1. Patrick Mahomes feels the backup offensive tackles Quarterback Patrick Mahomes looked uncomfortable from the pocket against the Seahawks, and it’s a reminder that his pocket presence and confidence can be temporarily skewed when he isn’t familiar with who’s protecting him. We’ve seen it throughout his career when backups are plugged in; it can take him time to adjust, and he didn’t seem to settle into this game until the fourth quarter. Mahomes finished with five yards per pass attempt and a 58.3 passer rating, the fifth-lowest marks of his career in both categories. Mahomes has played in 131 career games. Mahomes threw a handful of off-target passes in the first half, including two weirdly bad throws to tight end Travis Kelce. There was another deep attempt to wideout Xavier Worthy that was severely short and inside. At one point, Mahomes threw five straight incompletions, including an interception. On a second-and-10 play late in the second quarter, Mahomes rolled out left and tried to throw into a tight sideline window, but he rushed it as safety Nick Emmanwori bore down. A lack of a proper shoulder turn let the pass float into the safety’s hands over the top. On third-and-7 later in the third quarter, Mahomes stepped up and out of a messy pocket but didn’t account for a Seattle pass rusher as he tried to run to the sideline with the ball out and away from his body. The Chiefs fortunately recovered the ensuing fumble, but it was an example of Mahomes not playing like himself in Seattle. The offense struggled overall, but Mahomes failed to elevate his play to make up for shortcomings around him. That includes taking care of the ball; two turnovers by the signal caller are unacceptable in a low-scoring defensive battle. 2. There has to be a solution for covering slot receivers Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba proved further that he is one of the best offensive players in the game on Sunday night. Two of his biggest plays were incredible catch-and-throws down the sideline over cornerback Mansoor Delane. The rookie fought hard on both, but Smith-Njigba outplayed him on two big-time plays. That will happen. The Chiefs’ defense needed to do better at preventing Smith-Njigba — and other Seattle receivers — from catching quick throws over the middle. That happened an inexcusable number of times on Sunday night. The Seahawks started the game 9/11 on third downs by leaning on middle-of-the-field throws to Smith-Njigba and Cooper Kupp. The primary culprit for Kansas City was cornerback L’Jarius Sneed. His physicality off the line, disrupting routes and timing, is less useful in the slot when receivers have a two-way go and aren’t usually lined up on the line of scrimmage. After a game like this, it begs the question: does either Delane or Nohl Williams need to start seeing slot coverage reps? Sneed may be more sound in boundary coverage. At one point, the Chiefs threw Kristian Fulton at Smith-Njigba in the second half. Sneed was not on the field for a third-down stop at the start of the fourth quarter. Adjustments in the secondary may already be underway. 3. The Chiefs lost the third-down battle on both sides It was easy to see the Chiefs’ defense struggled to get off the field, and the offense mirrored that by starting 0/5 on third down and finishing 3/11. Kansas City didn’t advance past Seattle’s 40-yard line until four minutes remained in the third quarter. The Chiefs' first points come with 1:42 left on the clock in the third quarter. This is the latest the Chiefs have ever opened their scoring in a Patrick Mahomes *regular season* start Their first points in the 2024 Super Bowl v. the Eagles came with 0:43 left in the 3rd — Benjamin Solak (@BenjaminSolak) October 26, 2026 Emmanwori broke up a third-and-one rollout by reading the play at the snap and covering both Mahomes’ scrambling and Walker as a pass option. It was a reminder that this Super Bowl champion defense is elite in every respect, including knowing an offense’s tendencies. The Chiefs manufactured very little open space. On third-and-8 in the second half, Kansas City went to a screen pass to Walker to set up a fourth-and-short conversion. It reflected the lack of open targets downfield all night, especially on pass downs. As a result, Walker had to carry the load for the team’s pass catchers as a check-down option. He finished with a team-high four catches, but only for 21 yards. Tight ends Travis Kelce and Noah Gray combined for six catches for 85 yards. The backs and tight ends were Mahomes’ only outlets in Seattle; the Chiefs’ wide receivers combined for 39 yards on 13 targets. We’ll see whether a matchup with the Denver Broncos ‘ pass defense is more fruitful for the team’s receivers, or whether general manager Brett Veach will be active before the trade deadline on November 10th. 4. The Chiefs should bring in competition for Harrison Butker Harrison Butker’s two misses in this game were crucial. Before halftime, after cornerback Nohl Williams intercepted and returned the ball to set up a last-second attempt, Butker left a 58-yard field goal short. After hitting a 50-yard field goal to get Kansas City on the board in the second half, the Chiefs looked to Butker to bring the game within one possession with less than nine minutes to go. He pushed the 45-yard field goal wide right, dooming any comeback attempt by keeping the score at 13-3. If Butker’s range is limited, on top of being unreliable from mid-range, the team will need to be honest with itself about trusting Butker in important games later on in this season.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Final score: Chiefs fall to Seahawks for first loss of season
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night, falling 20-3 to the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field. Kansas City dropped to 5-1 after being held to 210 total yards, 11 first downs and a 3-for-10 conversion rate on third down. Seattle accumulated 388 yards, converted 11 of 15 third downs […]
full_text: (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night, falling 20-3 to the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field. Kansas City dropped to 5-1 after being held to 210 total yards, 11 first downs and a 3-for-10 conversion rate on third down. Seattle accumulated 388 yards, converted 11 of 15 third downs and controlled possession for more than 32 minutes. Seattle led 10-0 at halftime behind Jason Myers’ 25-yard field goal and Sam Darnold’s 28-yard touchdown pass to Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Patrick Mahomes threw an interception to Ty Okada, but Nohl Williams prevented further damage by intercepting Darnold near the goal line and returning it 64 yards. Kansas City failed to capitalize when Harrison Butker’s 58-yard attempt came up short. Butker’s 50-yard field goal produced the Chiefs’ only points in the third quarter. He later missed from 45 yards, and Emanuel Wilson’s 21-yard touchdown run extended Seattle’s advantage to 20-3. The Seahawks limited Kansas City to 50 rushing yards, including a quiet homecoming for former Seattle running back Kenneth Walker III, and then sealed the game by running out the clock. Kansas City will return home looking to rebound from its lowest-scoring performance of the season. Join Arrowhead Pride on game day! Stay on top of every Chiefs update and debate every snap with other members of Chiefs Kingdom. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . First Quarter Kansas City crossed midfield on its opening possession behind an 18-yard completion from Patrick Mahomes to Cyrus Allen. The Chiefs appeared to convert third-and-7 with a 12-yard pass to Kenneth Walker III, but an illegal-shift penalty on Travis Kelce erased the gain. Facing third-and-12 after the penalty, Mahomes threw incomplete down the left side to Kelce, bringing on the punt team. Matt Araiza then punted 36 yards, with Rashid Shaheed making the fair catch at Seattle’s 15-yard line. Seattle leaned heavily on its running game, using five different ball carriers to move from its own 15 to the 42. Jaxon Smith-Njigba gained five yards on an end-around and later converted third-and-5 with a nine-yard reception, while tight end AJ Barner moved the chains with a direct snap on third-and-1. Kansas City’s defense eventually forced a third-down incompletion from Sam Darnold, and Michael Dickson’s 48-yard punt was fair-caught by Nikko Remigio at the Chiefs’ 10. Kansas City put together a balanced drive from its own 10, with Kenneth Walker III carrying four times and Patrick Mahomes completing passes to Justin Watson and Noah Gray. Gray made the biggest play, hauling in a 19-yard reception to move the Chiefs across midfield. The drive stalled at Seattle’s 42 after Xavier Worthy gained only two yards on second down and Mahomes’ third-down pass to Worthy fell incomplete under pressure from Derick Hall. Matt Araiza’s punt was fair-caught by Rashid Shaheed at the Seahawks’ 7. Second Quarter Seattle marched 93 yards from its own 7, converting three third downs along the way. Sam Darnold found Cooper Kupp for 11 yards before connecting with Jaxon Smith-Njigba for gains of 10 and 33 yards, the latter moving the Seahawks to Kansas City’s 20. Seattle reached the 6-yard line, but the Chiefs’ defense tightened: Alohi Gilman and Nick Bolton dropped AJ Barner for a one-yard loss before George Karlaftis pressured Darnold into a third-down incompletion. Jason Myers made the 25-yard field goal to give Seattle a 3-0 lead Kansas City opened the possession with a five-yard pass from Patrick Mahomes to Kenneth Walker III, followed by a four-yard Walker run. After Mahomes’ third-down pass to Walker fell incomplete, the Chiefs kept the offense on the field, and Walker converted fourth-and-1 with a three-yard run to the Seattle 46. Mahomes then missed Travis Kelce under pressure from Leonard Williams before Nick Emmanwori pressured him into an interception intended for Jalen Royals. Ty Okada returned the pick one yard to Seattle’s 33, ending Kansas City’s most promising possession. Seattle turned Patrick Mahomes’ interception into a 10-play, 66-yard touchdown drive. Jaxon Smith-Njigba gained eight yards on an end-around, Emanuel Wilson converted second-and-13 with a 15-yard reception and Sam Darnold scrambled seven yards to move the chains on third-and-6. On third-and-9 from the Kansas City 28, Darnold found Smith-Njigba deep down the left side, where he was initially ruled out at the 1-yard line. Replay showed Smith-Njigba reached the end zone before stepping out, changing the play to a 28-yard touchdown and giving Seattle a 10-0 lead. Kansas City’s offense went three-and-out after taking over at its own 35 with 1:44 remaining. Patrick Mahomes threw consecutive incompletions to Jalen Royals and Travis Kelce before a five-yard completion to Emmett Johnson left the Chiefs short of the marker. Matt Araiza’s 56-yard punt reached the Seattle 4, but Rashid Shaheed returned it 32 yards to the 36, giving the Seahawks favorable field position. Sam Darnold quickly moved the Seahawks into scoring range. He connected with Jaxon Smith-Njigba for gains of 21 and 28 yards, placing the ball at Kansas City’s 2-yard line. After Mansoor Delane and Drue Tranquill dropped George Holani for a one-yard loss, George Karlaftis pressured Darnold into an end-zone interception intended for Smith-Njigba. Nohl Williams returned the pick 64 yards to Seattle’s 44, preventing the Seahawks from extending their 10-0 lead before halftime. Following Nohl Williams’ 64-yard interception return, Kansas City had only seven seconds to capitalize before halftime. Kenneth Walker III gained four yards to the Seattle 40, but Harrison Butker’s 58-yard field-goal attempt came up short as time expired. The Chiefs entered halftime trailing 10-0 despite Williams’ late takeaway. Third Quarter Seattle opened the second half with a 14-play, 57-yard drive that drained nearly seven minutes from the clock. Sam Darnold converted third downs with a 10-yard scramble and a 12-yard pass to George Holani before finding AJ Barner for 19 yards to reach the Kansas City 12. The Seahawks advanced to the 6, but Nick Bolton and Mansoor Delane dropped Velus Jones Jr. for a six-yard loss, and a delay-of-game penalty pushed Seattle back even farther. Jason Myers finished the possession with a 35-yard field goal, extending the Seahawks’ lead to 13-0. Kansas City answered with a 13-play drive that consumed more than six minutes. Xavier Worthy converted fourth-and-1 with a two-yard catch, and Patrick Mahomes later found Travis Kelce for 18 yards on third-and-7 to move the Chiefs to Seattle’s 33. A 15-yard reception by Kenneth Walker III was erased by offsetting penalties, and Derick Hall then sacked Mahomes and forced a fumble that Mahomes recovered at the 32. Harrison Butker converted the ensuing 50-yard field goal, cutting Seattle’s lead to 13-3. Fourth Quarter Seattle picked up eight yards on its first two plays, but a false-start penalty on center Jalen Sundell turned third-and-2 into third-and-7. Sam Darnold then completed a short pass to Jaxon Smith-Njigba for only two yards, forcing a punt that Nikko Remigio fair-caught at the Kansas City 13. Kansas City drove from its own 13 to the Seattle 27 behind a pair of 19-yard completions from Patrick Mahomes to Travis Kelce and Noah Gray. An offensive-holding penalty created second-and-20, but Emmett Johnson gained 12 yards on a reception before Mahomes scrambled nine yards to convert third-and-8. The drive stalled after Andrew Armstrong gained three yards and Mahomes’ third-down pass to Cyrus Allen fell incomplete. Harrison Butker then pushed the 45-yard field-goal attempt wide right, leaving Seattle’s lead at 13-3 with 8:37 remaining. title: An ESPN report sheds negative light on Chiefs’ Josh Simmons saga
summary: On Sunday morning, more than 12 hours before kickoff between the Kansas City Chiefs and Seattle Seahawks on “Sunday Night Football,” ESPN released a significant report about left tackle Josh Simmons (back) days after the 2025 first-round pick was placed on the Reserve/Injured list. According to ESPN’s Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport, on Wednesday, Simmons […]
full_text: Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Sunday morning, more than 12 hours before kickoff between the Kansas City Chiefs and Seattle Seahawks on “Sunday Night Football,” ESPN released a significant report about left tackle Josh Simmons (back) days after the 2025 first-round pick was placed on the Reserve/Injured list. According to ESPN’s Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport , on Wednesday, Simmons “was told to leave” a team meeting by head coach Andy Reid and quarterback Patrick Mahomes. The report says Simmons “was sitting with his feet up” during the meeting with offensive personnel, prompting Reid to ask him to put his feet down. Simmons “pushed back” and cited back and hip aches as his defense. Apparently, this exchange “disrupted” the meeting enough for both Reid and Mahomes to direct Simmons to leave in order to receive treatment for the pain he was experiencing. Simmons “apologized to Reid and team leadership” by acknowledging that he could have handled it better, according to the sources. On Wednesday, he did not participate in practice after the incident at the meeting. The team cited personal reasons, and Vice President of Sports Medicine and Performance Rick Burkholder shared insight on what Simmons spent Wednesday doing : talking with his representation about how to proceed. “After discussion with Josh yesterday, we gave him some time to talk with his family and representatives to investigate next steps as he goes through this process, and that’s why he was listed as both personal and with the back injury… he took the day off to get with his people.” “It was decided and agreed upon by everybody — his people, his agent, him, myself, Andy, and Veach — that he should be placed on IR to give him more time to return to full function. He’ll continue with the rehab process with the goal of returning to play at the high level that he achieved in the past.” Just last week, Reid described Simmons’ return to play as a “ramp-up” period. After Wednesday’s incident, he was suddenly shut down. If the IR placement was all about rehabilitation “plateauing,” it’s just a coincidence that it hit a standstill the day he got into a disruptive back-and-forth with his head coach and quarterback? ESPN says “multiple sources” who witnessed the interaction shared the information, which is rare for the buttoned-up Chiefs. How did this information reach insiders when we rarely hear anything from Kansas City? It feels intentional, like members of the organization want to leave Chiefs Kingdom with a bad taste in their mouths about Simmons instead of simply continuing with the excuse of a hard-to-navigate back injury. Nothing about this saga has been positive for Simmons’ availability this season or his future as the franchise’s left tackle. However, before Sunday morning, it was easy to chalk it up to his fragility, a known risk when the franchise drafted him out of Ohio State in 2025. Now, fans will question Simmons’ character because it sounds like the Chiefs already are.

title: Chiefs-Seahawks: 5 things to watch in Week 7 matchup
summary: The undefeated (5-0) Kansas City Chiefs will take on the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks (3-3) on “Sunday Night Football” this week. The game kicks off at 7:20 Arrowhead time and will be broadcast on NBC. The Chiefs are off to a hot start and sit atop the AFC. Last week, they defeated the […]
full_text: (Photo by Soobum Im/Getty Images) | Getty Images The undefeated (5-0) Kansas City Chiefs will take on the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks (3-3) on “Sunday Night Football” this week. The game kicks off at 7:20 Arrowhead time and will be broadcast on NBC. The Chiefs are off to a hot start and sit atop the AFC. Last week, they defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 22-6 at home in a dominating defensive effort. The story of Kansas City so far has been running back Kenneth Walker —128 rushing yards and two touchdowns last Sunday — who leads the NFL with 665 rushing yards in just five games. The Seahawks have had a bumpy start as the defending champions. They have lost back-to-back games and have failed to create offensive consistency. Quarterback Sam Darnold has been picked off four times in the back-to-back losses, and no Seattle player has rushed for over 100 yards this season. Even with the offensive inconsistency, they still boast one of the best defensive units in the NFL, capable of keeping them in any game. Here are five things to watch. 1. Walker’s return The reigning Super Bowl MVP will make his return to the team that drafted him. Walker put up decent numbers during his first three seasons in Seattle, but midway through last season and into the postseason, he showed off his ability at the highest level. Seattle elected to bring back other players, and now Walker will have a chance to play for his former team. The Seahawks’ run defense is rugged, and they have not allowed a 100-yard rusher in almost two seasons, ranking 10th in the NFL, giving up around 96 yards on the ground per game this season. #Seahawks run defense when not using heavy boxes: -0.19 EPA/rush (6th) 33.0% success rate (5th) 0.77 yards before contact/carry (2nd) https://t.co/fLOagfzlCj — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 21, 2026 Two weeks ago, they held San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey under 100 yards, but he averaged 6.8 yards per carry on eleven touches. The cracks are there, and it will be a battle of minds between head coaches Andy Reid and Mike Macdonald. It will also be interesting to see if Walker recalls his former general manager’s remarks at their Super Bowl parade. This just became a cursed clip. Drunk John Schneider: “Kenneth Walker tried negotiating with me five minutes ago. It was really weird.” pic.twitter.com/cUZkKu1e6G — Polymarket Football (@PolymarketBlitz) September 15, 2026 2. Right tackle Once again, the Chiefs offensive line will be under heavy scrutiny as yet another backup will earn a shot to start the game. Jaylon Moore suffered a concussion in last week’s win and missed the entire week of practice. This will mean that reserve tackle Josh Ezeudu is projected to make the start on the right side. A five-year veteran in the NFL, Sunday night will mark Ezeudu’s 11th career start and first with the Chiefs. After spending the offseason as a member of the New York Giants , who drafted him in 2022, Ezeudu was traded to Kansas City following the conclusion of the preseason, and around the time that news of Josh Simmons’ back injury started to circulate. Josh Ezeudu LT Quick out of his stance into his drive and catch; meets the edge at the bend point on the arc and washes him past the QB. Good pass set path and good quickness to get there. pic.twitter.com/axAyHFEqJE — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) August 26, 2026 Ezeudu was fine in the snaps he played on Sunday, but the Seattle defensive front will be a tough task. The Seahawks have eight players with at least one sack, and three players with three. In a hostile environment, I would expect Andy Reid to use a well-timed quick game and screens to help lighten the load. 3. Stopping Smith-Njigba Through the early portions of the season, Smith-Njigba has solidified himself as the league’s top receiver and leads the league in catches, yards, and touchdowns. He has eclipsed the century mark in five of six games so far this season, but this week he faces a different kind of test. Chiefs DB coach Dave Merritt on Jaxon Smith-Njigba: “He's the best receiver that we've seen without a doubt… We have a lot of press and off-coverage tape on him… We are mindful of the fact that we need to have all eyes on him." ( @goldmctNFL ) — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) October 22, 2026 As Kansas City Chiefs defensive coordinator, Steve Spagnuolo has found ways to keep the game’s top receivers under wraps. Last season, the Chiefs allowed one receiver to go over 100 yards — Nico Collins of the Houston Texans in Week 14 — and this season they have yet to allow a 100-yard receiver. Cornerbacks Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane have been fantastic so far this season, but Smith-Njigba presents a much larger challenge. I expect the Chiefs to use a combination of Williams and Delane to double-cover Smith-Njigba and not allow him to get going. Jaxon Smith-Njigba did EVERYTHING he could to keep Seattle alive in Denver. 12 REC, 134 REC YDS, 11.2 AVG vs Broncos Even in the loss, JSN kept coming through every time Seattle needed a big play. pic.twitter.com/BXpWnSdUA5 https://t.co/g2cWBUkgRc — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) October 16, 2026 4. Harrison Butker The Chiefs kicker is off to a rough start to the season, but against a high-level defense such as Seattle’s, the Chiefs will need a big night from their kicker. Butker is 10-for-13 on field goals this season and 14-for-15 on extra points, but he struggles when kicking beyond 50 yards. He is just 1-for-4 on 50+ yard field-goal attempts, and this has put the defense on short fields. While he’s been automatic inside the 50, these misses from distance have fueled speculation about his future with the team after this season. The team appears to remain internally confident, and with a catalog of historic kicks, it would take a series of unexpected blunders to force the Chiefs’ hand in season. In the #Chiefs 22-6 win over the Chargers, K Harrison Butker missed 1 FG and 1 extra point. Andy Reid tells @SorenPetro , "Whatever the problem is, he'll fix it and get it taken care of. He works like crazy at that." pic.twitter.com/WimYH0RHw7 — Sports Radio 810 WHB (@SportsRadio810) October 19, 2026 5. WRs and return man With the Chiefs’ receiver room depleted by injury, multiple players saw an uptick in snaps this past week, which should put internal pressure on return man Nikko Remigio. Last week Remigio struggled, fumbling a punt that was recovered by the kicking team, and his lack of snaps in the offense raises questions about his value on the team when the Chiefs need as many bodies as possible ready to go at receiver. Backup returner Brashard Smith is out this week with a hamstring injury, so Remigio will get the reins this week, but I would imagine the pressure to perform will be elevated. The Chiefs signed Andrew Armstrong to the active roster on Friday after elevating him a week ago, and this should mean more snaps for him in the offense alongside Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals, and Cyrus Allen. Remigio will need to quickly lock back in on what has kept him on the roster, but the clock is running, and if the Chiefs look to outside help at wide receiver, he will likely be the odd man out. Remigio has had one thing keeping him around and he’s been playing with fire today. — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 18, 2026

title: What did we learn from Rams’ win over Raiders?
summary: Even with a win Sunday over the Las Vegas Raiders, the Los Angeles Rams’ path to the playoff is still narrow. It will likely take 10 wins to earn a wildcard berth in the NFC playoff picture. The mission entering Sunday was 8-3. Now it is 7-3. That’s not to take away from LA’s impressive […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - OCTOBER 25: Puka Nacua #12 of the Los Angeles Rams celebrates after a first down against the Las Vegas Raiders during the first quarter at Allegiant Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images Even with a win Sunday over the Las Vegas Raiders , the Los Angeles Rams’ path to the playoff is still narrow. It will likely take 10 wins to earn a wildcard berth in the NFC playoff picture. The mission entering Sunday was 8-3. Now it is 7-3. That’s not to take away from LA’s impressive win over the Raiders. The defense fared well despite missing Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, Poona Ford, Kobie Turner, and Nate Landman. They will get some reinforcements over the coming weeks, although Ford has been ruled out for year. Sunday also brought the offense’s most well-rounded performance of the season so far. Matthew Stafford was efficient . Blake Corum and Kyren Williams churned out yardage on the ground to stay ahead of the chains. The Rams’ win over the Raiders doesn’t mean nothing. It’s encouraging. But it will take more in order to get where the team aspires to be. LA likely needs to win its next three games over the Los Angeles Chargers, Washington Commanders, and Arizona Cardinals in order to give themselves a chance over a daunting backend stretch. Keep losing teams losing. Stack blocks and eventually you’ll end up with a skyscraper. Here are four things I learned from Sunday’s victory: #1 – Deep passing game is still broken Where did the 20+ yard passes go in the offense? The offense line is allowing sufficient time to throw downfield. Defenses are strategically trying to take this play away, but one of the best offensive architects in Sean McVay should still be able to draw up favorable matchups. One absence that looms large is Terrance Ferguson. The pass catching tight end has been on injured reserve since Week 3. There are conflicting reports as to how soon he will be back. The Rams might not be able to push the ball downfield effectively until Ferguson returns. Will someone else step up in the meantime? #2 – Replacing Davante Adams in the aggregate The Rams don’t have someone of Adams’ caliber on the roster who can step in an immediately replace the future hall of famer. They also don’t have any reserve receivers who look ready for a key role within the offense. Jordan Whittington and Konata Mumpfield have been very disappointing given the ample opportunity they’re afforded. At least against Las Vegas, Colby Parkinson seemed to replace Adams between the 20’s and then Davis Allen filled in for red zone duties. Parkinson finished with 48 yards on five catches. Allen caught two touchdowns. That’s a typical Adams stat line when Puka Nacua is healthy. The mix could look different next week. At least the Rams have proof of concept for now. #3 – An unexpected upgrade at linebacker? Nate Landman missed Week 7 because of the NFL’s concussion protocol. Shaun Dolac filled in and performed admirably. Did Dolac make a splash play like Landman’s trademark punchouts? No. He was stingy in coverage and held up in run defense despite his slight frame. Dolac’s athleticism was a welcome addition to the middle layer of the defense. The Rams may want to consider making Dolac a full-time player in this defense, or at least give him more opportunity to earn the job. #4 – A reserve defensive lineman in the spotlight Poona Ford is out for the year. Kobie Turner will be on injured reserve for a while. Still, the Rams held the Raiders to 42 yards on 14 carries (3.0 average). Are the Raiders a great running team? Far from it. But Ford and Turner’s absences did not turn into a glaring weakness. The reason for that? Likely Tyler Davis, who has been an underappreciated defender for LA in recent years. He’s a starting quality player who is getting his first opportunity. He doesn’t look keen on squandering what is in front of him.
