title: Steelers stock report after Week 7 win over Saints
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers defeated the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the NFL’s first game in Paris, France. It was a day in which points were hard to come by, but it felt as though the Steelers were in control from start to finish. As always, here is my weekly stock report after the Steelers moved […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers defeated the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the NFL’s first game in Paris, France. It was a day in which points were hard to come by, but it felt as though the Steelers were in control from start to finish. As always, here is my weekly stock report after the Steelers moved to 5-2 on the season. Stock up RB Jaylen Warren Warren came into the contest already one of the most efficient running backs on a per touch basis in the NFL, and today was no exception. Warren carried the ball 18 times for 101 yards, good for 5.6 yards per carry. The back added three receptions for 36 yards to his line. After posting over 100 scrimmage yards in the first half, it was a quiet second half for offense in general. On a day where there weren’t many explosives on either side, Warren was once again the engine that kept the Steelers offense moving. Even with Dowdle increasingly involved, Warren is the clear leader in the Steelers running back split. ​TE Darnell Washington The Steelers’ best play in the red zone is when they throw the fade route to Darnell Washington. On his only target of the game, Washington used his six-foot-seven-inch frame to dunk on a Saints defender and bring down the ball for the Steelers’ only touchdown of the game. In a game in which the Steelers struggled to get into the end zone, Washington was their only sign of life. The tight end has become a dependable red zone threat with three touchdowns this season and counting, the most of his career. ​Defense Many online have dubbed this the Steelers’ “bend don’t break” defense, and the nickname feels appropriate. Because of the sheer amount of zone coverage they run, opposing quarterbacks have found soft spots and moved the ball downfield. Tyler Shough finished with an efficient 30/38 passing line, but the Steelers defense held New Orleans to just 10 points. The Saints have struggled to run the ball all season long, and Pittsburgh took advantage of that as they only allowed 18 yards on the ground. Pittsburgh had two forced fumbles called narrowly called back, and were always looking to punch the ball out and be aggressive. Patrick Graham deserves a lot of credit ​Stock Down Finishing Drives The Steelers actually put themselves in positions to score throughout the game after struggling to move the ball much at all last week in Tampa Bay. However, the Steelers could not find the end zone and had to often settle for field goals. Aaron Rodgers was visibly upset on the sidelines in the fourth quarter after having to settle for their third field goal of the game. It might not seem like much of an issue today since they emerged victorious, but the offense will need to turn those field goals into touchdowns if they want to seriously compete for anything down the stretch of the season. ​TE Pat Freiermuth The Steelers tight end had a quiet day with only two catches for 20 yards, but many of the Steelers’ pass catchers had quiet days today. Freiermuth had a crucial drop in the fourth quarter that would have set the Steelers up deep inside Saints territory. It was a well-placed ball by Rodgers, but the tight end was unable to come down with it. As we just talked about, if the Steelers want to compete with the rest of the AFC, they will have to clean up small mistakes like this that force them into field goal situations rather than scoring touchdowns. ​Throwing fade routes to DK Metcalf This is not so much about DK Metcalf as it is about how much the Steelers tried to use this play today. Early in the red zone, the team called Metcalf’s number on a fade route, but the ball was simply uncatchable. Later in the first half, Rodgers tried to hit Metcalf on a similar play, but the ball was uncatchable again. The Steelers tried the play once again later in the game, and while the ball was catchable, it fell incomplete. Fade routes are a thigh-risk, high-reward kind of play that is fine in moderation, but it became the definition of insanity as they continued to call it. On a day in which points were hard to come by, it might have been smart to opt for higher percentage throws, especially in the red zone. Or, give your six-foot-seven tight end more opportunities on those routes. Metcalf had a fine day overall, in which he led the team in yards and caught a downfield post route for a chunk gain of 51. title: Steelers punish Saints on the ground, win 16-10 in Paris
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers rode their run game to a third consecutive victory, defeating the New Orleans Saints 16-10. The Steelers are now 5-2, and are now tied with the Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs for the most wins in the AFC. From the opening drive, the Steelers made it clear they would ride the […]
full_text: (Photo by FRANCK FIFE / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers rode their run game to a third consecutive victory, defeating the New Orleans Saints 16-10. The Steelers are now 5-2, and are now tied with the Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs for the most wins in the AFC. From the opening drive, the Steelers made it clear they would ride the run game against a Saints’ defense that entered the game with the worst run defense in the NFL in terms of EPA. Jaylen Warren totaled 43 yards on the ground on the first drive, but the Steelers stalled out after an incomplete fade to DK Metcalf in the end zone, Chris Boswell made it a 3-0 game. The first quarter would see only one drive a piece, as the Saints punted following an 11-play drive. Pittsburgh one-upped them with a punt after a 13-play drive. The Saints put a field goal on the board to even the score, which then led to the Steelers driving 77 yards in six plays on a Darnell Washington touchdown grab. The touchdown pass was the 540th of Aaron Rodgers’ career, which moved him ahead of Peyton Manning into third place. The Saints answered back, though, with a 12-play drive that ended on a Devaughn Vele touchdown on 4th-and-goal from the one yard-line. The Steelers scored on their ensuing drive, adding another Boswell field goal to go up 13-10. And just as it looked like the Saints were about to score another touchdown, the game flipped. Payton Wilson picked off Tyler Shough in the red zone, killing what could have been a drive that tied the game or put New Orleans up by a score. The Steelers would add a third Boswell field goal to go up 16-10, and the Saints would never reach the red zone again. Daniel Carlson missed a 52-yard field goal, and New Orleans would go four plays and punt the next time they had the ball. The Steelers took over with just under six minutes left in the game, and wouldn’t allow New Orleans to touch the ball again. A Rodgers third-down scramble led to the Steelers running the clock down to a minute left, and an offsides call on the Saints on a fourth Boswell field goal allowed the Steelers to kneel the game out to get their fifth win. In the keys to victory, we talked about the Steelers needing to lean into the run game and being efficient on third down. Well, they out-rushed the Saints 148-18 and were 10-of-16 on third down. Jaylen Warren rushed for 101 yards and added 36 yards through the air. Rico Dowdle added 41 yards rushing and 45 yards receiving, respectively. On defense, Patrick Queen had a strong day, racking up a team-high 10 tackles and a sack on what was the final offensive play for the Saints. T.J. Watt added a sack, and Pittsburgh had six tackles for loss on the day. The Steelers will host the Browns next week with a chance to get to 6-2 ahead of their Week 9 bye week. title: NFC Playoff Picture: Seahawks climb back into NFC West race with win, 49ers loss
summary: We’re not quite halfway through the 2026 NFL season, but the next time the Seattle Seahawks play a game will be November, so we might as well take a look at where they stand in the playoff hunt after their Week 7 win over the Kansas City Chiefs. What makes Seattle’s win over the Chiefs […]
full_text: We’re not quite halfway through the 2026 NFL season, but the next time the Seattle Seahawks play a game will be November, so we might as well take a look at where they stand in the playoff hunt after their Week 7 win over the Kansas City Chiefs . What makes Seattle’s win over the Chiefs doubly important is the fact that the San Francisco 49ers lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons, ending their undefeated run as they enter a bye week. While it would’ve been cool for the Los Angeles Rams to keep slumping and lose to the Las Vegas Raiders, that did not materialize, but they’re still behind the Seahawks in the NFC West battle. The Arizona Cardinals also lost. NFC West standings after Week 7 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1, 3-0 NFCW) 2. Seattle Seahawks (4-3, 1-1 NFCW) 3. Los Angeles Rams (3-4, 1-2 NFCW) 4. Arizona Cardinals (2-5, 0-3 NFCW) In the bigger picture, the Seahawks are still out of a playoff spot due to the insane depth of the NFC North, in which every team is above .500. It’s not a thing to worry about right now, but it seems more likely than not that the NFC North will be the main competition for Seattle in terms of the Wild Card hunt. NFC playoff standings after Week 7 1. Minnesota Vikings (6-0) 2. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 3. New York Giants (4-2-1) 4. Carolina Panthers (3-3) 5. Chicago Bears (5-2) 6. Detroit Lions (4-2) 7. Green Bay Packers (4-3) – Currently has tiebreaker on Seahawks due to better record vs. NFC (3-3 vs. 1-2) 8. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 9. Atlanta Falcons (3-4, 3-2 NFC) 10. Los Angeles Rams (3-4, 2-2 NFC) 11. Philadelphia Eagles (2-4) – Monday Night Football 12. Dallas Cowboys (2-4) – Monday Night Football 13. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-5, 1-0 NFCS) 14. New Orleans Saints (2-5, 0-1 NFCS, 1-3 NFC) 15. Arizona Cardinals (2-5, 1-4 NFC) 16. Washington Commanders (1-4-1) Damn, that Commanders loss just really looks so annoying compared to Seattle’s other losses. But there’s still a lot of ball left, and the Seahawks still have reason to set their sights on the NFC West instead of effectively limiting their scope to the Wild Card chase.

title: Winners and Losers from Seahawks vs. Chiefs: ‘The Dark Side’ destroys Patrick Mahomes
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are in the win column again after a complete shutdown of the Kansas City Chiefs offense. While the final score was 20-3, the game was much more lopsided than that, and better red zone offense would’ve led to an even more emphatic scoreline. Given the San Francisco 49ers loss earlier in the […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are in the win column again after a complete shutdown of the Kansas City Chiefs offense. While the final score was 20-3 , the game was much more lopsided than that, and better red zone offense would’ve led to an even more emphatic scoreline. Given the San Francisco 49ers loss earlier in the day, this was a massive opportunity for the Seahawks to get back into the NFC West race and turn their season around. They took full advantage and reminded everyone that when they keep the mistakes to a minimum, they’re still one of the NFL’s best. Let’s get to Winners and Losers! Seattle Seahawks Winners There’s nobody better at wide receiver right now than Jaxon Smith-Njigba Could I lead with anybody else? By halftime he had 6 catches for 129 yards and a touchdown, and it really should’ve been 8/142/1 if not for a couple of screens that were thrown as laterals. His final stat-line was 9/150/1 to continue his outrageous follow-up season to his Offensive Player of the Year 2025 season. We will soon be talking about JSN not just as one of the best receivers in the NFL, but one of the best receivers to have ever played the game. And in an ideal world, he’ll spend every single one of those seasons as a Seattle Seahawk. Emanuel Wilson grinds out a workmanlike 100-yard performance If Kenneth Walker not getting 100 yards (or really being all that effective at all) was not some earth-shattering surprise going up against the vaunted Seattle run defense, who had Emanuel Wilson going for 100? The bulk of his bulldozing came in the fourth quarter when the Chiefs defense was worn out and Wilson had time to work. His 21-yard touchdown run gives him his fourth overall TD on the year, and he’s well on pace to set a career high in rushing yards. Wilson’s role is simple: north-south, physical runner who can give you some help as a receiving back. He’s not flashy but he’s a playable back with the right blocking and right play-calls. When Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price return, Wilson should still get some touches. Sam Darnold, even with the interception, played very well By the time I hit publish on this article I will be under the covers and snoring my life away. I fully expect some dissenting voices as far as putting Sam on the Winners list because of how bad that end zone interception was. There’s no excusing the pick, but it was also more or less the only blemish on a highly efficient night. He got the ball out quickly, on time, and accurately. He scrambled for critical first downs, didn’t take any sacks, and outside of the pick he also wasn’t forcing doomed passes into tight coverage. Darnold looked comfortable and in control of the offense almost all night, and his deep balls to Jaxon Smith-Njigba were a thing of beauty to watch. I can live with Darnold’s brain cramps when he’s largely productive and playing winning football. It’s the preceding two weeks in which Darnold becomes a liability more than the solution. Tonight, Darnold looked a lot more like 2025 Darnold, and he did so against a Steve Spagnuolo defense. Brian Fleury (somewhat) quiets the critics Speaking of Seahawks under fire, Brian Fleury needed the offense to look cohesive and functional. I won’t pretend it’s perfect and I won’t pretend it’s optimal to constantly have to convert third and medium or long, but would you rather they show they can convert in obvious passing situations or not? I thought so. Fleury had answers for situations in which the offense had struggled, and he outfoxed Spags. A lot of the offensive woes have been poor player execution, but I don’t think Fleury has put the Seahawks in the best positions to succeed. He did a much better job settling Sam Darnold early, using play-action more efficiently even in lower volume, and using the run game to help limit the possessions in the game. Kansas City had few opportunities to respond, whereas the Seahawks did enough with their possessions. There’s still a lot to work on as far as getting plays in quicker and not short-circuiting in the low red zone, but I was very happy with the flow of the game. Perhaps that mini-bye was the breather Fleury and Sam needed to figure some things out. I’m eager to see if this is more than a one-off and the start of legitimate improvement after a rocky start. stuff @TheHawksEyePod has been talking about, but off the broadcast it felt like on the deeper drops the progression within their common concepts was adapted to the coverage more or at least Sam was finding those windows way earlier. Basically, They Got Good. https://t.co/cl3m6HZYp6 — under zone x (@cmikesspinmove) October 26, 2026 George Holani did some dirty work you’ll appreciate later Holani had a pivotal third down conversion when he broke two tackles on a checkdown. That’s not the play I want to focus on. Holani had a key block on Darnold’s second scramble for a first down, but he also slowed down Nohl Williams on the interception runback, which allowed Charles Cross to make the tackle. In effect, Holani helped save at least a touchdown and assured the Chiefs could only muster up a long field goal attempt (which was missed). That’s winning football. That’s 12 as One. Holani didn’t wow with his touches outside of his catch, but he won in the margins when he didn’t have the ball. A.J. Barner gets more involved You wanted the Barnyard? You got it three times and it worked every time. Barner also had four catches for 42 yards, so he finally was more involved in the passing game as a receiving threat. He was a tipped ball away from probably scoring a touchdown in the second quarter. Happy National Tight Ends Day, A.J! The offensive line did its job and then some No sacks, only two quarterback hits allowed, and zero holding penalties. Anthony Bradford coming back provided some stabilization if only for communication purposes, not necessarily blocking performance in itself. This was a tough assignment dealing with Chris Jones and George Karlaftis while facing Spags’ blitzes, and the Seahawks OL won the challenge. Nick Emmanwori is a monster I don’t think Emmanwori has played a better game in his young career than Sunday night. He hassled Mahomes into an interception, covered Xavier Worthy down the field, played the run well, he did everything you’d want out of your Apex superstar. There were a couple of times he was caught out of position on an improvised Mahomes scramble to a tight end, but Mahomes does that to everyone. If Emmanwori had some sort of hip thing before this game that led to a questionable designation, he could’ve fooled me in terms of how healthy he looked. Emmanwori must love synth-pop because he was in full Erasure mode tonight . Ty Okada lives for Sunday nights To date, Okada has two career interceptions. Both have come in spectacular fashion on SNF. Seattle has undeniably had issues replacing the depth they lost at edge and running back, but Coby Bryant’s exit has stung far less because Okada (and Rodney Thomas II when Ty was injured) is a more than capable starting safety. Tyrice Knight continues filling in nicely for Drake Thomas The first play of the game, T-Knight got juked out by Kenneth Walker. He had Walker in his hip pocket the remainder of the night, closing up holes and doing an exemplary job with his run fits throughout the night. Seattle’s linebacker depth was once a question mark at the start of 2025 (outside of Ernest Jones IV, of course). It is now a position of quiet strength. Derick Hall leads the pass rush Whew! I’ve been harsh on Seattle’s edge group for not being productive enough, but after a slow start the Seahawks edges capitalized on Kansas City’s backup tackles. Hall was outstanding and recorded a strip sack, plus he had several pressures. Hell, even Dante Fowler Jr was doing stuff! Mahomes was sacked just once but you could feel that DeMarcus Lawrence, Hall, Uchenna Nwosu, and Fowler were speeding Patrick up. Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy dominate Want to know why K9 could barely do…

title: Seahawks vs. Chiefs post-game reaction video: What we learned from Seattle’s masterful performance
summary: The Seattle Seahawks aren’t to be buried just yet, as a national audience found out on Sunday Night Football. Not only did the Super Bowl champions crush the Kansas City Chiefs offense all night, the offense looked cohesive, competent, and as free-flowing as it’s really looked all season. Over 400 yards of offense, 11/16 on […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks aren’t to be buried just yet, as a national audience found out on Sunday Night Football . Not only did the Super Bowl champions crush the Kansas City Chiefs offense all night, the offense looked cohesive, competent, and as free-flowing as it’s really looked all season. Over 400 yards of offense, 11/16 on third downs, and no sacks allowed was vital. But that defense? Wow. Patrick Mahomes has never quarterbacked an offense that inept until tonight . Join myself and Bryce Coutts for live post-game reaction to Seattle’s versus the Kansas City Chiefs. We’re starting up at about 9:00 pm PT and should run for a little over an hour. We’ll be watching the comments section and our own YouTube chat. Seahawks vs. Chiefs: What we learned The Seahawks defensive dominance is a reminder that this is still an elite unit . The Seahawks defense didn’t even let the Chiefs get into the red zone, never mind the end zone. Kenneth Walker had just 36 yards rushing and zero explosive plays, while Patrick Mahomes rarely looked comfortable in the pocket and he couldn’t find open receivers on time with regularity. Emanuel Wilson can still have a role in this offense even when Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price return . If Walker not having a big night isn’t a major shock, who had Wilson with 100 yards on 24 carries and a game-sealing touchdown? While Wilson didn’t have too many huge plays in terms of explosive runs (outside of the TD), his physical running style seemingly wore the Chiefs defense down until they finally broke. Sam Darnold and Jaxon Smith-Njigba are still a lethal combination . Darnold’s awful interception aside, Sam looked as good and as comfortable in this offense as he’s had all season. He scrambled for timely first downs, made several clutch throws on third down, and his chemistry with Jaxon Smith-Njigba is still superb. JSN had 9 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown, with 13 rushing yards due to two Darnold throws going down as laterals. The offense looked more functional, even if there were some tough moments . As mentioned at the top, the Seahawks hummed on third down, had long, time-consuming drives, and they showed a lot more cohesiveness. Turnovers were kept to just the one from Darnold, no one fumbled, and the time of possession battle skewed heavily in Seattle’s favor. Perhaps there are positive signs that the mini-bye was a get-right moment for both Darnold and Brian Fleury, but we’ll need to keep seeing improvement over the next few weeks to be sure. Video

title: Seahawks defense holds Patrick Mahomes to the worst offensive performance of his career
summary: The Seattle Seahawks completely shut the Kansas City Chiefs offense down in a glorious 20-3 win at Lumen Field. While the offense limiting the turnovers, converting timely third downs, and holding up in pass protection were keys to a pivotal victory, the Seahawks’ Super Bowl-winning ‘Dark Side’ defense deserves the main headlines. If not for […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks completely shut the Kansas City Chiefs offense down in a glorious 20-3 win at Lumen Field. While the offense limiting the turnovers, converting timely third downs, and holding up in pass protection were keys to a pivotal victory, the Seahawks’ Super Bowl-winning ‘Dark Side’ defense deserves the main headlines. If not for Patrick Mahomes recovering his own fumble in one of the wildest scrambles you’ll ever see, the Chiefs might have been shut out for the first time in any Mahomes start. It was only the fourth time a Mahomes-led offense failed to reach the end zone, and it was a night of firsts in terms of offensive ineptitude for the three-time Super Bowl champion. Kansas City never reached the red zone, which was a first for the Mahomes era in the regular season or playoffs. But wait, there’s more fun with numbers! The Seahawks held the Chiefs to their fewest points (3, tied), total yards (213), first downs (11), and red zone drives (0) in any game started by Patrick Mahomes. — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) October 26, 2026 Technically, the Chiefs did have just 212 yards of offense in a playoff win over the Houston Texans, but when 18 yards were lost on an intentional safety I think we can call the Seahawks performance the official lowest yardage total in a Mahomes start. Yes, Kenneth Walker was a big storyline coming into Sunday night. He had just 36 yards on 14 carries, but he also just got there and the Seahawks have the stingiest run defense in the NFL. Patrick Mahomes has almost a decade worth of gaudy offensive numbers, such that it’s jarring to see him look so frazzled and bereft of answers. This is not unlike the Super Bowl losses to the Philadelphia Eagles and Tampa Bay Buccaneers for Mahomes, but his first time playing ‘The Dark Side’ ended in a night he’ll want to quickly forget. Mike Macdonald’s defenses tends to do that. THAT'S TY'S BALL 🔥 @tyokada 's first INT of the season. 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/VI76EKHkC4 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 FORCED IT 💥 @derick_hall9 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/JAHEpYix98 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 One to forget for Kansas City! The Chiefs had their joint-fewest points (3), fewest Red zone drives (0), and 2nd-fewest yards (213) in any of the 153 games started by Patrick Mahomes, regular season or playoffs. Mahomes was pressured on 19 of 36 dropbacks (53%), the 4th-highest… pic.twitter.com/OnsMT3TLAk — ESPN Insights (@ESPNInsights) October 26, 2026 If you’re keeping score, the only other time Mike Macdonald coached against Mahomes was the AFC Championship when the Chiefs beat the Baltimore Ravens. KC only scored a field goal in the second half, which means Macdonald defenses haven’t allowed a TD against Mahomes in six consecutive quarters.

title: Seahawks-Chiefs score: Seahawks shut Patrick Mahomes, Kenneth Walker down in dominant win
summary: The Seattle Seahawks (4-3) needed a win in the worst way, and what a way to pull it off. They dominated the Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) from start to finish, and the 20-3 Seahawks final score actually flattered the Chiefs. It wasn’t Kenneth Walker who rushed for over 100 yards; he only had 36 yards […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks (4-3) needed a win in the worst way, and what a way to pull it off. They dominated the Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) from start to finish, and the 20-3 Seahawks final score actually flattered the Chiefs. It wasn’t Kenneth Walker who rushed for over 100 yards; he only had 36 yards on 14 carries. It was Emanuel Wilson, whose fourth quarter touchdown wrapped things up, who led everyone with his first 100-yard game as a Seahawk. It wasn’t Sam Darnold who looked frazzled and panicked (outside of one throw, admittedly), it was Patrick Mahomes. Darnold was 20/28 for 257 yards, a touchdown, and an aforementioned bad interception that ultimately didn’t result in any Chiefs points. Most importantly, Darnold was not sacked. Mahomes threw for only 165 yards, an interception, and multiple times the NBC cameras showed him looking in disbelief playing “The Dark Side” defense. Kansas City never reached the red zone, a first in the Mahomes era. Seattle had over 400 yards of total offense, with Jaxon Smith-Njigba responsible for 150 through the air and another 13 in rushing yards. The Seahawks may have dropped two straight, but they bounced back and reminded everyone that they’re still the Super Bowl champions until further notice. Seahawks vs. Chiefs 1st half recap The Chiefs started on offense and, in a surprise to no one, looked to get Kenneth Walker involved early. Walker caught a pass for six yards on the opening play, and was set to convert a third down through the air on a checkdown. Travis Kelce, however, never got set and was called for an illegal shift. A throw from Patrick Mahomes to Kelce was off-target, resulting in a punt after just one first down gained. Seattle’s sputtering offense got the ball at its own 14. Jaxon Smith-Njigba was targeted on the first three plays, catching two passes for 14 yards. AJ Barner converted on a ‘Barnyard’ special, but the Seahawks drive stalled out after Tory Horton couldn’t reel in a third-down pass from Sam Darnold. Mansoor Delane knocked the ball loose for an excellent PBU. While the Chiefs were backed up inside the 10, the usual Mahomes magic saw him escape the pocket to hit a couple of throws to Justin Watson and Noah Gray. Derick Hall took advantage of Kansas City’s backup right tackle to force a throwaway from Mahomes on third down and short in Seattle territory. Andy Reid, probably predictably, went against modern day philosophies and punted instead of go for it at Seattle’s 43. The Seahawks were pinned at their 8. The Seahawks scored the opening points of the night, albeit not nearly as many as they would’ve liked. Sam Darnold was crisp on a 15-play, 86-yard drive that included multiple third-down conversions to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, plus one to Cooper Kupp. The second JSN conversion was an explosive play for 27 yards into the red zone. COMPLETE TO JSN 😮‍💨 @jaxon_smith1 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/stAo8YBsfy — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 Velus Jones Jr scampered for 11 yards on the right side of the line to set up a goal-to-go sequence that was one to forget. A.J. Barner’s shovel pass bubble thankfully stayed in his hands, but there was only a field goal at the end of the road. Jason Myers was spot on from 25 just outside the midway mark of the second quarter. 3-0 Seahawks. PICK! The first interception thrown in this game was by Mahomes, not Darnold! Nick Emmanwori pressured Mahomes, who stumbled while scrambling and threw a bad ball into the waiting arms of Ty Okada. It’s his second career interception, both coming on SNF! THAT'S TY'S BALL 🔥 @tyokada 's first INT of the season. 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/VI76EKHkC4 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 The Seahawks made their way into Chiefs territory through first downs by Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Emanuel Wilson, but the highlight entering the two-minute warning was Sam Darnold scrambling out of pressure and diving for the first down. A 7-yard gain on 3rd and 6 to keep the drive going! Darnold gets creative with his feet to pick up a much-needed first down 😤 KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/gwEQThEY3y — NFL (@NFL) October 26, 2026 On 3rd and 9, Darnold beat the blitz by attacking 1-on-1 coverage down the field. You know who caught it, you know who scored it (upon replay review). 10-0 Seahawks. SUNDAY NIGHT SPECIAL 🗣️ Touchdown @jaxon_smith1 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/gO0GLrO7uJ — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 The Chiefs two-minute drill cratered quickly, with Mahomes looking uncomfortable and rushed, both mentally and physically. A three-and-out followed by a good punt return by Rashid Shaheed gave the Seahawks a chance at more points before halftime. Darnold kept dealing, throwing another dart to JSN to set up first-and-goal at the 2. George Holani was stuffed at the 2, then the follow-up pass by Darnold was picked in the end zone by Nohl Williams. This could’ve been a game-changing pick-6 if not for the efforts of Charles Cross, who chased Williams down to not just prevent the touchdown, but keep KC out of automatic field goal range. NOHL WILLIAMS END ZONE INT AND A BIG RETURN KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/K42foMAhQy — NFL (@NFL) October 26, 2026 K9 got a short run that almost ran the clock out, but the Chiefs had a timeout and a second left. Harrison Butker’s 58-yarder was straight but short, so the score remained 10-0 Seahawks at halftime. Seahawks vs. Chiefs 2nd half recap The Seahawks failed to score in their two-minute drill when they were right at the doorstep, so no opportunity to double up. They did get the ball to start the second half, and once again they were able to capitalize on third down, something they’ve struggled to do all year. Darnold scrambled for a first down into Chiefs territory, then George Holani broke two tackles for another first down on 3rd and long! A play-action throw to A.J. Barner put the Seahawks in the red zone, where things inevitably went awry. No turnover this time, so Jason Myers came on for a 35-yard field goal. 13-0 Seahawks. Kansas City finally got the ball back for an extended period of time and got into field goal range, in part because Mahomes converted 4th and short to Xavier Worthy, followed by his usual scramble drill with Travis Kelce. On third down, Mahomes was sacked and rocked by Derick Hall, who forced the ball out. Seemingly the entire Seahawks defense and Chiefs offense had a chance to recover the ball, and somehow Mahomes recovered it! Harrison Butker made a field goal, so that recovery saved three points. 13-3 Seahawks. FORCED IT 💥 @derick_hall9 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/JAHEpYix98 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 The Seahawks got a big kick return from Tory Horton to near midfield, but squandered the field position and punted it back. The Chiefs needed points and they needed them pronto. Mahomes hit a couple of big throws to Travis Kelce and Noah Gray. Kansas City worked its way into field goal range, then Leonard Williams swatted a 3rd and 3 pass down to make Andy Reid decide between another 4th down attempt or kicking a field goal. He trusted Harrison Butker from 45 yards out and he was not to be trusted. Wide right! Seattle got the ball back and went into clock-killing mode. Not only did they kill clock, they killed the game. Throws to JSN and A.J. Barner gained first downs, while Emanuel Wilson provided the knockout punch. He found a crease between Nick Kallerup and Eric Saubert for the 21-yard touchdown run. 20-3 Seahawks. That was niiiiice 😮‍💨 TOUCHDOWN EMANUEL WILSON. 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/YfJgdXKJ4Y — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 26, 2026 The Chiefs turned it over on downs, Seattle ran the clock out, game over! Seahawks injury report WR/KR Rashid Shaheed was ruled out with a knee injury suffered in the second quarter. RB/KR Velus Jones Jr was ruled out with a hamstring injury suffered in the third quarter. title: Seahawks injury updates: Rashid Shaheed, Velus Jones Jr ruled out
summary: The Seattle Seahawks will be down a couple of players for the remainder of their Week 7 game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Wide receiver Rashid Shaheed was ruled out with a knee injury after colliding with Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a Sam Darnold interception just before halftime. Shaheed was not out there for the start […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks will be down a couple of players for the remainder of their Week 7 game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Wide receiver Rashid Shaheed was ruled out with a knee injury after colliding with Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a Sam Darnold interception just before halftime. Shaheed was not out there for the start of the second half and otherwise had his special teams return duties assumed by Tory Horton. Meanwhile, a thin running back room got even thinner when Velus Jones Jr left in the second half with a hamstring injury. He’s now out for the game, which leaves the Seahawks with only George Holani and Emanuel Wilson as the available backs for the rest of the evening. #Seahawks WR Rashid Shaheed (knee) will not return, while RB Velus Jones Jr. is out because of a hamstring injury. — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) October 26, 2026 The Seahawks enter the fourth quarter with a 13-3 lead over the Chiefs, and if they are to pull off a critical win, they’ll have to do it with an undermanned offense.

full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have their backs against the wall. They have only lost three straight once under Mike Macdonald, and that was back in the pre-Ernest Jones part of the 2024 season. The reigning Super Bowl champions are 3-3, struggling on offense, and dealing with some key injuries on both sides of the ball. What’s not a pleasant sight to see is the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs and their league-leading rusher, a fella by the name of Kenneth Walker III. Can the Seahawks offense stop turning the ball over? Can they finally look good on third down? Will the defense be able to stymie their former teammate and prevent him from rushing for over 100 yards again? Will Seattle’s pass rush do anything to fluster Patrick Mahomes? Is Sam Darnold going to continue playing bench-worthy football or will he snap out of his funk? title: Familiar MVP candidates will meet on ‘Sunday Night Football’ in Seahawks vs. Chiefs
summary: We may be witnessing a showdown of the two most effective offensive weapons in the NFL today. One is the reigning Super Bowl MVP, and the other is the reigning Offensive Player of the Year. Kenneth Walker III has exploded to elite production to begin the 2026 NFL season. He leads the league in rushing […]
full_text: We may be witnessing a showdown of the two most effective offensive weapons in the NFL today. One is the reigning Super Bowl MVP, and the other is the reigning Offensive Player of the Year. Kenneth Walker III has exploded to elite production to begin the 2026 NFL season. He leads the league in rushing yardage (665 through only 5 games), most runs of 20+ (7), runs of 40+ (2), owns the longest rushing gain in the league (76), has the 2nd-highest rushing TD total by a back (6), and has 0 fumbles, while the 5 guys ahead of him with the most attempts in the NFL all cannot say that. Jaxon Smith-Njigba has, himself taken his play to another level. He leads the league in receiving yards (717) and receiving touchdowns (7), is second in both most catches of 20+ (10) and catches of 40+ (2) yards, owns the longest receiving gain in the league (82), is tied for 4th in receiving YAC by a wideout (he and Zay Flowers both have 210 yards) and among the top 15 WR’s in catches, he has the highest 1st down percentage (73.5%). He remains the biggest (and sometimes it feels like only) threat on the Seahawk offense, and yet still cannot be stopped by opposing teams. We all know that the MVP award is usually just the best QB award… but these two monsters deserve to win it if they keep up their individual paces. If nothing else, these are the two front runners for the 2026 OPOY award. In one less game this season than his former Seattle team, Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker III has rushed for more yards and touchdowns than all the Seahawks RBs combined. But Seahawks WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba has more receiving yards and receiving touchdowns than all Chiefs WRs combined.… pic.twitter.com/NidGjMuhlJ — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 25, 2026 You read that right: “Both players are on pace to set the NFL single-season rushing and receiving records” (respectively). Two absolute superstars and unique chess pieces who just won a Super Bowl together. Yes, we all wish Ken was still in Seattle, but he needed this opportunity to shine this brightly as the focal point of an offense. It is amazing that Seattle housed both players last year, and even mixed in Zach Charbonnet. Both players are facing defenses that seem equipped to handle them. Seattle faces Walker as the 4th-ranked defense at defending the run (3.5 yards per carry) and have not allowed a 100-yard rusher in a franchise record, and the NFL’s longest active streak: 35 games straight. Kansas City will be covering Smith-Njigba while ranked #1 in DVOA against teams’ WR1. The caveat with that last part is that they’ve squared off against the Broncos, Colts, Dolphins, Raiders and Chargers. Not exactly a murderer’s row of dominant wideouts. Although, KC’s rookie corner does deserve some recognition. Mansoor Delane has been LIGHTS OUT pic.twitter.com/iPiGhJ4sXp — PFF (@PFF) October 21, 2026 Whichever of these two playmakers: K9 for KC and JSN for SEA that can tilt the field the most, may just lead his team to a victory. The “Dark Side”, of course, will have something to say about things. Byron Murphy, Ernest Jones IV (an important matchup) and Julian Love are truly balling on all three levels and will be tasked with neutralizing their former teammate on the field.

title: Adam Schefter: Seahawks among teams ‘expected to consider’ Jonathan Taylor trade
summary: The Indianapolis Colts’ 2026 season has gone far from how they’d hoped, leaving them in a position to potentially sell off their stars for draft picks. One of those stars has repeatedly come up in fan conversations surrounding the Seattle Seahawks: running back Jonathan Taylor. However, it appears that it might not all be speculation, […]
full_text: The Indianapolis Colts’ 2026 season has gone far from how they’d hoped, leaving them in a position to potentially sell off their stars for draft picks. One of those stars has repeatedly come up in fan conversations surrounding the Seattle Seahawks: running back Jonathan Taylor. However, it appears that it might not all be speculation, as ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported on Sunday that the Seahawks are one of four teams that have “pondered, or are expected to consider, the possibility of a trade for the star running back.” If they want the 27-year-old running back, the Seahawks would be competing with the Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers and the Denver Broncos, according to Schefter’s report. Aside from the vague language there, a trade for Taylor makes sense on its face for the Seahawks. Taylor has been a premier back in the NFL since joining the Colts in 2020, is a three-time Pro Bowler and is coming off a season where he ran for 1,585 rushing yards and scored 18 touchdowns. With rookie Jadarian Price on IR and Zach Charbonnet out, there’s certainly hunger in Seattle to get their running game back on track. Seattle has spent most of their season rocking with Emmanuel Wilson and George Holani, who have struggled to generate a consistent, quality rushing offense. The issues with trading for Taylor emerge when looking at the value needed to acquire him and the contract extension that Taylor signed in the offseason. Taylor is owed $7 million in base salary in 2026, which balloons to $16 million in 2027 and then $18 million in 2028. For a franchise that, under general manager John Schneider, has not paid many running backs, that could be a tough sell. Notably, in Schefter’s report, the Seahawks are not explicitly tied to Colts All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson. All the NFL insider mentions in his article are that the 30-year-old offensive lineman could be on the market, with several “playoff-worthy” teams interested. The trade deadline sits on Nov. 10, so the Seahawks will have more time to ponder as they look to battle past a 3-3 start and continue their reign over the league.
author: Jack Freeman

title: 49ers News: Pain
summary: 49ers ‘took a step back’ in first loss of season against Falcons“Losing is never great, but when you do lose, I think especially in this organization, it makes everybody really just look at yourself in the mirror,” Kittle said. “It’s definitely going to sour our entire bye week, and I think that’s good because I […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 25: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers scrambles with the ball against the Atlanta Falcons during the fourth quarter at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers ‘took a step back’ in first loss of season against Falcons “Losing is never great, but when you do lose, I think especially in this organization, it makes everybody really just look at yourself in the mirror,” Kittle said. “It’s definitely going to sour our entire bye week, and I think that’s good because I think when we get back next week, I think our guys are going to be incredibly focused. “Would I rather win? Absolutely. Way more fun. But hey, like I said, it could be worse. We didn’t have a bunch of guys get injured today. I think we made it out pretty healthy. And we got guys coming back, so I’m excited about that.” 49ers go a-stumbling into the bye (paywall) “The secondary was terrible, especially Ji’Ayir Brown and Jack Jones. Brown was late to everything. Jones didn’t know his job, held on almost every play, and got benched for Ephesians Prysock. The 49ers played a bunch of Cover 3, and Atlanta was more than happy to eat up the underneath yardage. But it was no Mike Evans eventually broke down the structure of the offense. So much was decided by every single choice route being wrong. Brock Purdy could not seem to get on the page with anyone, even Christian McCaffrey. Everyone broke in too early, or out too late, or kept going when he expected them to sit. In an offense predicated on timing and expectations, that can mean doom.” Kawakami: What needs fixing and what definitely doesn’t as the 49ers hit the bye (paywall) “The 49ers cannily played the long-game this weekend by not pushing Mike Evans and Nick Bosa out there when they weren’t 100% healthy; and they had Upton Stout in uniform only on an emergency basis — then suffered for it when Jack Jones got torched again and again. But can you imagine if the 49ers played any of those guys, perhaps aggravated their nagging injuries, and still lost? This game was on a short week on artificial turf after a long flight on a 10 a.m. body-clock start. They’ll never say this, but the 49ers knew they could afford a loss on Sunday. And if the 49ers (who outgained the Falcons 400-295) didn’t commit four turnovers, they still easily could’ve won this game, anyway.” Despite 49ers’ hot start, changes loom at kicker, CB, WR and perhaps D-line (paywall) “ Some of the names being bandied about — Josh Sweat, Khalil Mack, Daron Payne and DeForest Buckner — would be strong additions, and Buckner certainly would fit the homecoming theme the 49ers have struck all year with one-time players like Samuel and Dre Greenlaw. Heading into the weekend, multiple reports said the Indianapolis Colts would hold off on a fire sale to see whether they could reverse their freefall in coming weeks. On Sunday, they lost to the Minnesota Vikings 16-10, dropping their record to 2-5. Buckner, a 2016 first-round pick of the 49ers, is in the final year of his contract and is still beloved by the San Francisco fan base, the front office and those who played alongside him. He currently has four sacks, which would lead the 49ers.” 49ers’ depleted WR corps contributes to Brock Purdy’s forgettable day: ‘That’s a real thing’ (paywall) “ The beat-up wideout corps meant Purdy was operating with a stripped-down game plan devised by Shanahan and offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak.” 3 Winners and 11 Losers from the 49ers’ loss to the Falcons “ I didn’t watch Week 7 thinking, “Purdy cost the 49ers the game.” There was an objectively bad decision on an interception that should’ve ended up in the 10th row. If you’ve ever played quarterback, it’s one you’ve probably thrown because you thought you had more space along the sideline than you actually did — and probably because you waited too long to decide who to throw the ball to. Purdy had dropback on the drive before where he scrambled, and it felt like he was in the pocket for 10 seconds. He bought enough time for his tight end and picked up a first down on what would’ve been third and long. On another play, Colton McKivitz was beaten cleanly off the line of scrimmage, which would result in a sack for 90% of quarterbacks. Purdy danced around the pocket just long enough before shoveling the ball to Jordan James, who ran for a first down—another second-and-long turned into a first down. The second interception is one you tip your cap to the Atlanta Falcons on a design that has gotten the best of Purdy throughout the years. Purdy finished in the top five this week among quarterbacks in success rate. His throws to Jordan Watkins, especially the one in the end zone, were on the money—the end-zone one is about as good a throw as you can make. He made a few different throws that were contested that his pass catchers did not haul in. They are the same throws we’ve taken for granted because Evans has caught them all year.”

title: NFC Playoff Picture: San Francisco 49ers lose but remain in the driver’s seat for the No. 1 seed
summary: The San Francisco 49ers suffered their first loss of the season. Here’s how the playoff picture and divisional standings shake out. NFC West standings before Week 8 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 2. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 3. Los Angeles Rams (3-4) 4. Arizona Cardinals (2-5) We’ll have a more thorough update about the division first […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers suffered their first loss of the season. Here’s how the playoff picture and divisional standings shake out. NFC West standings before Week 8 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 2. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 3. Los Angeles Rams (3-4) 4. Arizona Cardinals (2-5) We’ll have a more thorough update about the division first thing Monday morning, but here’s a look at the standings. The 49ers are 3-0 in the division. Seattle is 1-1. The Rams are 0-2 — something that could come back to bite them down the line. NFC playoff standings after Week 7 1. Minnesota Vikings (6-0) 2. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 3. New York Giants (4-2-1) 4. Carolina Panthers (3-3) 5. Chicago Bears (5-2) 6. Detroit Lions (4-2) 7. Green Bay Packers (4-3) 8. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 9. Atlanta Falcons (3-4, 3-2 NFC) 10. Los Angeles Rams (3-4, 2-2 NFC) 11. Philadelphia Eagles (2-4) – Monday Night Football 12. Dallas Cowboys (2-4) – Monday Night Football 13. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-5, 1-0 NFCS) 14. New Orleans Saints (2-5, 0-1 NFCS, 1-3 NFC) 15. Arizona Cardinals (2-5, 1-4 NFC) 16. Washington Commanders (1-4-1) The 49ers have a date with the Vikings in a few weeks. So they’ll have an opportunity to regain the No. 1 seed. The Niners would also have the head-to-head advantage over Minnesota if it came down to a tiebreaker at season’s end. A quick look at the Vikings’ schedule makes you think they’ll be lucky to make the playoffs, let alone earn a bye. Yes, they’re undefeated, but the Vikings face the Lions twice, Bills, Packers, Niners, Falcons, Panthers, Patriots, and Bears to end the season. Those are all coin-flip games. J.J. McCarthy leading the Giants to a division win would sum up the NFL: You never know what’s going to happen. McCarthy wasn’t great on a down-to-down basis, but he made a few big-time plays when New York needed him to. There’s still a lot of football to play. Carolina leads the NFC South, but they took it to the chin in Week 7. That division is far from solved. Tampa Bay’s defense looks for real. I wouldn’t count them out. Green Bay has the talent, but they are not a buttoned-up team. The Seahawks had over 400 yards against the Chiefs, but are you scared of that offense? Their defense is scary, but Sam Darnold is inevitable. The Falcons are inconsistent, but they’ve proven they can beat anyone on any given Sunday. They’re talented, but probably a year away. The longer the Rams stick around, the more chances they get to get healthy and make a playoff run.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 Winners and 11 Losers from the 49ers’ loss to the Falcons
summary: The San Francisco 49ers dropped their first game of the season against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7. The 49ers outgained the Falcons by 105 yards and by 1.5 yards per play. But seven penalties, four of which turned into first downs for the Falcons, plus four turnovers and a missed extra point, are how […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers dropped their first game of the season against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7. The 49ers outgained the Falcons by 105 yards and by 1.5 yards per play. But seven penalties, four of which turned into first downs for the Falcons, plus four turnovers and a missed extra point, are how you lose that game. When you’re already down your most impactful player on both sides of the ball, you can’t expect to beat anyone, let alone on the road in a short week. You can be frustrated with the performance and understand the sky isn’t falling. The 49ers are 6-1 and remain one of, if not the best, teams in the NFL. Sunday just wasn’t their day. Let’s take a look at the winners and losers from Week 7. Winners Fred Warner Warner finished with two tackles for loss and a couple of big stops that helped get the defense off the field. He finished with a team-high 13 tackles. Warner wasn’t targeted once. He only rushed the passer twice. That suggests Warner took away the middle of the field in coverage. Penix had two attempts over the middle of the field beyond 10 yards. Warner did his job. He’s playing the run as well as he has in his career. George Kittle The end-of-game fumble summed up the turnover battle. Don’t let that play cloud your judgment about how Kittle played. Kittle caught eight of his 10 receptions for 88 yards, and averaged five yards after the catch. He also caught both third-down targets for 21 yards. We knew Kittle would be heavily involved in the passing game. He was targeted at the fourth-highest rate among all tight ends in Week 7. Sumer Sports had Kittle with a team-high five impact plays. He proved that the 49ers offense could function without Mike Evans. Christian McCaffrey It’s the three best players to start here, but that’s how it should be when your depth is depleted. You should lean on your best players, and that’s what the 49ers did. McCaffrey finished the game with only seven carries, but that’s because of an injury and the 49ers having the ball only once in the third quarter. McCaffrey posted an incredible 71.4% success rate, gaining 25 yards after contact. He was the 49ers’ offensive weapon on their first drive of the game. McCaffrey finished with six receptions on seven targets for 61 yards. McCaffrey caught a contested target, and he also sprawled out along the sideline to reel one in. Brock Purdy I didn’t watch Week 7 thinking, “Purdy cost the 49ers the game.” There was an objectively bad decision on an interception that should’ve ended up in the 10th row. If you’ve ever played quarterback, it’s one you’ve probably thrown because you thought you had more space along the sideline than you actually did — and probably because you waited too long to decide who to throw the ball to. Purdy had dropback on the drive before where he scrambled, and it felt like he was in the pocket for 10 seconds. He bought enough time for his tight end and picked up a first down on what would’ve been third and long. On another play, Colton McKivitz was beaten cleanly off the line of scrimmage, which would result in a sack for 90% of quarterbacks. Purdy danced around the pocket just long enough before shoveling the ball to Jordan James, who ran for a first down—another second-and-long turned into a first down. The second interception is one you tip your cap to the Atlanta Falcons on a design that has gotten the best of Purdy throughout the years. Purdy finished in the top five this week among quarterbacks in success rate. His throws to Jordan Watkins, especially the one in the end zone, were on the money—the end-zone one is about as good a throw as you can make. He made a few different throws that were contested that his pass catchers did not haul in. They are the same throws we’ve taken for granted because Evans has caught them all year. Purdy was a big reason the 49ers were competitive on Sunday. Losers Eddy Pineiro After everything that went wrong, the 49ers could’ve had the ball with an opportunity to tie the game. But another Pineiro missed extra point put the 49ers in a predicament. The 49ers have been asking for it for multiple games with these misses. Pineiro’s only game without a missed kick was Week 2 against Miami. It nearly cost the team in Week 3. The next two games were closer because of Pineiro’s misses. In this one, the Niners couldn’t make up for another mistake by the kicker. The pass rush The defensive line ate some humble pie heading into the bye week. Michael Penix was pressured on 14.3% of his dropbacks, a Week 7 league low. We’ve grown accustomed to every player winning their 1-on-1 battles at least once or twice a game. That was not the case against Atlanta. This game should be a wake-up call for the 49ers that Osa Odighizuwa cannot be the defensive tackle who plays the most snaps for you. You won’t confuse him for a run defender, but the 49ers cannot afford a goose egg from Odighizuwa. He had a 0.0% pass-rush win rate, the same as Sebastian Valdez. Odighizuwa compounded his lack of impact with an unforgivable offside penalty on 4th and 4 before halftime. The penalty on James Thompson wasn’t his fault, but a penalty nonetheless. The edge group didn’t find success, either. Mykel Williams had a 12.5% pass-rush win rate. Nobody else was above 6%. And the combination of Mykel, Romello Height, and Keion White didn’t get a tackle for loss, but they did miss two tackles. The cornerbacks This performance feels like it’s been coming for a month now. This group hasn’t been sharp. The pass rush has been hiding them. When the pass rush doesn’t get home or even give the illusion of pressure, receivers end up running open and unchallenging. Everything the Falcons did felt…easy. The 49ers targeted the cornerbacks 12 times and allowed 9 receptions for 97 yards. The Falcons wideouts faced one contested catch. Sprinkle in a couple of ill-advised penalties at inopportune times, and you get a group that looks like they were the ones playing without multiple starters. The penalties The 49ers committed seven penalties for 55 yards, which may not sound like much on the surface, but they couldn’t have happened at a worse time. A false start on the first play from scrimmage foreshadowed what was to come. Odighizwua’s first offside penalty led to three points. Renardo Green had an illegal contact penalty on 2nd and 20. Jones was flagged for defensive holding on the same play. Thompson’s offside call was on 3rd and 2. McCaffrey had a 10-yard run negated by a holding penalty on Connor Colby to begin the fourth quarter. That led to a down-and-distance situation the offense couldn’t recover from. On 3rd and 4, when the game was 26-20, Brandin Cooks had a false start. Purdy’s second interception came on the next play. The turnovers The turnovers on the field were devastating for the 49ers. A promising drive ended when the young running backs fumbled on back-to-back plays, stripping the offense of a red-zone possession. The same offense that’s scoring at the highest clip in the league in the red area. That drive was going to answer Atlanta’s scoring drive. Purdy’s first interception came on Atlanta’s 25-yard line. He should have thrown it away and lived to fight another down. You can’t make that decision, especially when you’re in field goal range. The second interception came late in the fourth quarter with the offense around mid-field. Up until that point, it still felt like the 49ers would prevail. Kittle’s game-ending fumble was the football gods telling the 49ers Week 7 wasn’t meant to be. Contested situations A few differences separate a true WR1 from a role player. One is contested situations. Jacob Cowing caught one of his two contested catches. Jordan Watkins, who played well, all things considered, caught one of his three. The end zone reception would’ve been a difficult catch, but Watkins did the hard part. The same was true for the other target, who did everything but finish the…
author: Kyle Posey

title: Seahawks-Chiefs live discussion: Will another unbeaten team lose?
summary: The undefeated Kansas City Chiefs travel to Seattle to take on Sam Darnold and the Seahawks. The Chiefs will be without WR1 and WR2. They’ll also be without right tackle Jaylon Moore. The last place you want to be is short-handed against this Seahawks defense. We saw how they can prey on teams last year […]
full_text: (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The undefeated Kansas City Chiefs travel to Seattle to take on Sam Darnold and the Seahawks. The Chiefs will be without WR1 and WR2. They’ll also be without right tackle Jaylon Moore. The last place you want to be is short-handed against this Seahawks defense. We saw how they can prey on teams last year when the 49ers weren’t at full strength. But it’s Patrick Mahomes, and you’re asking for it by doubting him. It’ll be a tall task to come away victorious in Seattle. We saw what it took for the 49ers to win. Will it end differently for the Chiefs? Darnold has thrown an interception in three of the four games since he returned from injury. It would be news if Darnold didn’t turn the ball over at this point. Darnold gets a Chiefs defense that is ninth in the NFL in interception percentage. I see the Seahawks winning comfortably, 24-14, in an ugly game.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 takeaways from the 49ers loss to the Falcons: Too many self inflicted wounds
summary: The San Francisco 49ers finally fell from the undefeated ranks on Sunday, as they lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons on the road in Week 7, going to 6-1 on the season. San Francisco came into the game beaten up, as they had just four receivers active for the game with Mike Evans out. Still, […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 25: San Francisco quarterback Brock Purdy (13) passes the ball during the NFL game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Atlanta Falcons on October 25th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers finally fell from the undefeated ranks on Sunday, as they lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons on the road in Week 7, going to 6-1 on the season. San Francisco came into the game beaten up, as they had just four receivers active for the game with Mike Evans out. Still, they came into the game as 2.5-point favorites and had plenty of opportunities to win this one. But despite outgaining the Falcons by over 100 yards, they ended up on the wrong side of the game. Here are three quick takeaways from the 49ers 29-20 loss to the Falcons on Sunday. Self-inflicted wounds The margin for error for San Francisco was low heading into this game, and the 49ers had just too many self-inflicted wounds on both sides of the ball that proved costly. In the second quarter, up 14-9 with under five minutes left, the 49ers had Atlanta on 4th & 4 at the San Francisco 44-yard line. They gifted Atlanta a first down with an encroachment penalty from Osa Odighizuwa. As a result, the Falcons drive continued, and they got a field goal to end the half. Then, on a crucial drive to end the third and open the fourth quarter, with the 49ers down 19-14 needing a stop, they were trending in that direction, as the Falcons had a 2nd & 20 at their own 13-yard line. Well, the 49ers were flagged for both illegal contact and holding on the play, granting Atlanta another first down. Later on that same drive, the Falcons were on 3rd & 8 at their own 46-yard line. This time, Jack Jones, who was flagged for holding on the previous error, was called for pass interference, once again extending Atlanta’s drive. The errors on the drive didn’t stop there. The 49ers stuffed Bijan Robinson on 3rd & 2 at the San Francisco 26, but they had 12 men on the field and were also offsides on the play. Another first down. And on the following play, the 49ers gave up a 21-yard touchdown to Drake London. What could’ve been a quick punt ended up being an 11-play, 90-yard touchdown drive lasting over five and a half minutes that the 49ers couldn’t recover from. Down 12, it forced San Francisco to go for it on 4th & 10 at the Atlanta 23 on the next drive with over 11 minutes left, which ended in a sack. Late in the game, with the 49ers down six and facing a 3rd & 4 at the Atlanta 47, Brandin Cooks had a false start, backing the Niners up, and Brock Purdy had an interception on the next play. Then, perhaps one of the costliest miscues of the day was Eddy Piniero’s missed extra point on the 49ers final touchdown. Hitting that would’ve had the Niners down eight on their final possession, but the miss kept it a two-score game and highly unlikely for a comeback. Maybe it doesn’t matter anyways with George Kittle’s fumble, but that problem has been a recurring one for the 49ers special teams unit this year. San Francisco had seven penalties in this game, and a lot of them were in costly situations. Turnovers You’re very rarely going to win a game when you have four turnovers and the opposing team has zero. Well, the 49ers had a ton of chances to win this one, even in the final minutes, but their turnovers were all brutal, which was too much to overcome on top of the self-inflicted wounds. Up 14-9 in the second quarter and driving in Arizona territory, the 49ers got lucky when a Jordan James fumble was recovered by Luke Farrell, setting San Francisco up with a 2nd & 1 at the Atlanta 28. Well, it didn’t matter as Kaelon Black coughed the ball up on the next play. San Francisco was in scoring range and ended with no points. To make matters worse, Atlanta ate up the final 4:20 of clock, kicking a field goal to end the half and starting the second half with the ball, where they scored a touchdown. Major turnaround there. The 49ers’ second turnover also came with the Niners driving well into Atlanta territory. On 2nd & 14 from the Atlanta 25, Brock Purdy escaped the pocket, rolling to his right, and seemed to be trying to hit Jacob Cowing. But Cowing didn’t roll with his quarterback, and Purdy’s pass was intercepted by a diving Jesse Bates, who made a great play. Should Purdy have thrown this one away. Probably. Did Cowing also make a mistake? Looked like it. That’s another scoring opportunity wiped off the board, and Atlanta responded well, going 11 plays and 90 yards for a touchdown to extend their lead to 26-14. That five-possession swing was the ballgame. On top of the four turnovers, the 49ers also had the turnover on downs, which, once again, came on a drive where San Francisco was deep in Atlanta territory. Interestingly enough, the models said to kick on 4th & 10 at the Atlanta 23, but with the 49ers down 12 and the defense struggling to get a stop, Kyle Shanahan went for it and Brock Purdy was sacked. In hindsight, the 49ers have a shot if they kicked there, but the process also made sense from a go-for perspective. Then, San Francisco had a big chance to take the lead down six after the defense forced back-to-back three-and-outs. With just over four minutes left, the 49ers got the ball at their own 47-yard line. They got to a 3rd & 4, but Brandin Cooks’s false start pushed them back five, and the defense made a great play on Brock Purdy’s second interception, which essentially sealed the deal. It was a rough game for the 49ers, to say the least. Niners defense contains damage The 49ers defense had some back-breaking penalties in this one. But it was encouraging that they held Bijan Robinson to 63 yards on 20 carries, while also having a good game in the red zone. The 49ers forced three field goals in the red zone in this one, mitigating some of the defense, while they gave up only 4.7 yards per play. There were some long drives where the penalties hurt, and the 49ers could not get off the field. That needs to be cleaned up, as Atlanta had drives of 10, 14, 10, and 11 plays, resulting in 23 of their points. But on a day when the offense had four turnovers, there were some solid things to take away from Raheem Morris’s unit, as the coordinator tried to create a plan to disrupt the quick game of Michael Penix. Now, the secondary has been leaky two weeks in a row. There have been far too many penalties from that group, including a few that were killer in extending Atlanta drives. But this Atlanta rushing attack has been a hard one to stop, and the Falcons had been a top-five team in EPA per play since Penix returned to the starting lineup. So there were a few positives to take from a disappointing outing.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers lose to the Falcons in a game full of turnovers and mistakes
summary: The San Francisco 49ers offense wasted no time scoring, marching 64 yards in just over five minutes on 10 plays for a touchdown to start the game. Christian McCaffrey gained 16 and 24 yards on the drive. The Falcons took the ensuing kickoff 61 yards. Fred Warner made a phenomenal third-down tackle, bringing down Bijan […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers offense wasted no time scoring, marching 64 yards in just over five minutes on 10 plays for a touchdown to start the game. Christian McCaffrey gained 16 and 24 yards on the drive. The Falcons took the ensuing kickoff 61 yards. Fred Warner made a phenomenal third-down tackle, bringing down Bijan Robinson in the backfield for a three-yard loss. The Falcons settled for a field goal, making it 7-3. The Niners’ second drive stalled after Connor Colby surrendered a sack. This came after George Kittle picked up 17 yards on 3rd and 4. The Falcons also went three-and-out on a penalty. Christian McCaffrey missed the next drive. He ran up and down the sideline, trying to get loose. According to the broadcast, McCaffrey was dealing with a thigh injury. On the first drive without McCaffrey, rookie Kaelon Black ran for 15, 7, and a 30-yard touchdown to give the 49ers a 14-3 lead. The drive took 1:41 off the clock and came in just four plays. The Falcons answered with a touchdown on a 10-play, 68-yard drive. Atlanta’s kicker missed the extra point, making it 14-9. Jacob Cowing took a 10-yard reverse for a first down. Jordan James’ first carry of the game was a fumble that safety Xavier Watts appeared to recover, but Luke Farrell wrestled it away. Black fumbled on the second consecutive play. The 49ers weren’t fortunate enough to recover this one. The giveaway came on Atlanta’s 28-yard line on 2nd and 1. The Niners were bound to put points on the board. The Falcons took the rest of the first half with their next possession. They went to draw the Niners offsides with 29 seconds remaining. On 4th and 4, Osa Odighizuwa jumped offsides. Atlanta got a field goal out of the drive. The Falcons began the third quarter with the football. They did whatever they wanted on the drive, gaining 8, 10, and 12 yards before Michael Penix found Kyle Pitts for a 5-yard touchdown. That gave Atlanta a 19-14 lead. Jordan Watkins made the first wide receiver catch with just under nine minutes remaining in the third quarter. Watkins laid out for an impressive reception. Purdy kept the drive alive when there wasn’t anything there after scrambling. Kittle picked up a big chunk, then Farrell followed suit. But Purdy got a little too greedy on his next scramble. Instead of throwing the ball into the stands, he cut it close, and the Falcons intercepted it. This turnover came on Atlanta’s 25, squandering another scoring opportunity. The secondary continued to struggle. On 2nd and 20, Jack Jones committed an illegal contact penalty. On 3rd down, Bijan Robinson was uncovered on a coverage bust involving Dre Greenlaw, Jones, and Deommodore Lenoir. It looked like Greenlaw was in the wrong. Jones committed pass interference on 3rd and 8. James Thompson was offside on 3rd and 2, on a play where it looked like the 49ers got hosed by the substitution rule. Penix found Drake London down the seam on the next play, giving the Falcons a commanding 26-14 lead. The 49ers. gave Atlanta multiple first downs via penalty on the drive. The 49ers were aggressive on their next drive. Purdy found Watkins for 35 yards, but Connor Colby’s hold negated a 10-yard run by McCaffrey on the next play. Purdy threw a seed to Watkins in the end zone with perfect placement. But for the second time in the game, Watkins couldn’t secure the catch through the ground. An incomplete pass and a sack meant the 49ers would come away with no points on the drive. The Falcons helped the defense out on the next drive, after snapping the ball over Penix’s head. The 49ers got the ball back in 1:57. Purdy found Jacob Cowing for an 18-yard gain on the next drive. Cowing drew a defensive holding penalty two plays later. A 15-yard facemask by the Falcons pushed the ball deeper into Falcons territory. Kittle gained 11 yards to put the Niners at the 11. Purdy found McCaffrey just shy of the goal line, then threw to Kyle Juszczyk to make it a one-possession game, 26-20, after Eddy Pineiro missed the extra point. The defense forced a quick three-and-out. Atlanta shanked the punt. The offense had great field position, plenty of time, and all three timeouts. On 3rd and 4, Brandin Cooks flinched. That made it 3rd and 9. An underneath linebacker intercepted Purdy’s pass, sealing the game for the Falcons. That was San Francisco’s third turnover. Pineiro’s miss loomed large, as a Falcons field goal could make it a two-possession game. The Falcons tacked on a field goal to make it 29-20, all but ending the game. Fittingly, Kittle fumbled as the Niners were driving to make it a one-possession game.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers-Falcons live discussion: Brock Purdy and Kyle Shanahan will put up points
summary: The San Francisco 49ers will be without Mike Evans for the first time this season. According to warm-ups, Brandin Cooks and Jordan Watkins will start on the outside. Christian Kirk likely plays the slot, with Jacob Cowing sprinkled in there. When these teams met a season ago, Christian McCaffrey ran for 129 yards with Mac […]
full_text: (Photo by Scott Strazzante/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers will be without Mike Evans for the first time this season. According to warm-ups, Brandin Cooks and Jordan Watkins will start on the outside. Christian Kirk likely plays the slot, with Jacob Cowing sprinkled in there. When these teams met a season ago, Christian McCaffrey ran for 129 yards with Mac Jones as the starter. He also had seven receptions for 72 yards. In that game, George Kittle was held without a target. It’s national tight end week, so we think Kittle might be peppered with a target or five on Sunday. The wideouts who were targeted last year were Jauan Jennings — who had 31 yards on seven targets — Skyy Moore, and Kendrick Bourne. The 49ers only scored 20 points in that game, but it gives you an idea of how this offense can function, even without its starting quarterback, against the defense they’ll face today. Something tells me the 49ers will look like the 49ers once the game is decided. Can they contain Atlanta? Probably. This game could be high-scoring, as most 49ers games are.
author: Kyle Posey

Neither of those players […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers inactive list is out: QB Kurtis Rourke (3rd QB) DE Nick Bosa (calf) WR Mike Evans (Achilles) LB Luke Gifford (groin) WR Deebo Samuel (hamstring) S Marques Sigle (ankle) LB Garret Wallow (hamstring) The 49ers took the field in Australia with Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, Demarcus Robinson, and Deebo Samuel against the Rams. Neither of those players will be in uniform in Atlanta. It’ll be interesting to see how the 49ers use Christian Kirk and how often he plays. The 49ers are low on bodies to the point where rookie Enrique Cruz is active for the first time. While Cruz is unlikely to see action at offensive tackle, it paints a picture of how snake-bitten this team is by injury heading into Week 7. It’s worth noting the 49ers will have nine offensive linemen active. Last week, Kyle Shanahan moved Christian McCaffrey around the formation more than ever. It would not be surprising to see McCaffrey play more of a Cooper Kupp kind of role where he’s running a bunch of underneath routes to help the offense stay ahead of the chains. No Wallow or Gifford at linebacker, but Dre Greenlaw returns. That means Tatum Bethune and Jalen Graham will be special teamers. We’ll see if that makes a difference. Upton Stout is active after a shoulder injury that forced him to miss Monday Night Football. The secondary will be tested by Drake London, Bijan Robinson, and don’t sleep on Jahan Dotson against these cornerbacks.
author: Kyle Posey

title: NFL trade rumors: 49ers could make a run at Colts DT DeForest Buckner
summary: ESPN’s Adam Schefter tweeted early Sunday morning, “One team that could decide to make a run at Colts DT DeForest Buckner is the San Francisco 49ers, a team the star defensive tackle played for from 2016 through 2019, according to league sources.” In the article, Schefter and Ian Rapoport said, “NFL teams have been studying tape and […]
full_text: ESPN’s Adam Schefter tweeted early Sunday morning, “One team that could decide to make a run at Colts DT DeForest Buckner is the San Francisco 49ers, a team the star defensive tackle played for from 2016 through 2019, according to league sources.” In the article , Schefter and Ian Rapoport said, “NFL teams have been studying tape and discussing scenarios, trying to figure out if there is a way to acquire players from a Colts roster that includes running back Jonathan Taylor, guard Quenton Nelson, and defensive tackles DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart, according to sources.” According to the article, the Colts will try to win the next three games against the Vikings, Jaguars, and Cowboys before the November 10 trade deadline to give their coaches and players a chance to earn their way into the playoff mix. If that plan doesn’t go well, the Colts brass will deal resources and build for the future. The Packers, Seahawks, Broncos, and Vikings were teams listed as interested in Taylor. Only one team was listed for Buckner: The 49ers: The 49ers traded Buckner to the Colts in March 2020 for the 13th overall pick in that year’s draft. Buckner is now 32, playing as well as he ever has and scheduled to be a free agent in 2027. It makes him a prime target at a position several contenders need. Buckner already has been paid $10 million in a roster bonus, and he is due the rest of his $13 million base salary this year. Nearly guaranteed to leave Indianapolis after the season, a decision to unload players would almost certainly include Buckner. Buckner is a game-changer. Nothing has changed since he last played for the 49ers. He’s the second-best defensive tackle with four sacks. He’s top 10 in pressures and impact plays, and 11th in run stops. Under Raheem Morris and in the 49ers’ scheme, you can’t help but think that Buckner would be even better. With Buckner in the final year of his contract and not enjoying life in Naptown, the Colts have little leverage. The 49ers wouldn’t have to part with a first- or second-round pick. He’s 32, so we’re not talking about a four-year extension or anything. But according to Sports Info Solutions, Buckner is the third-most valuable defensive lineman in the NFL by their points-saved metric. Here’s what was said about Nelson: Still one of the NFL’s best guards, Nelson is only 30 and entering the final year of his contract. Though he expressed interest in a long-term deal with Indianapolis, Ballard never was able to finalize one that certainly would have paid Nelson at the top of the market at his position. Similar to Buckner’s situation, there are several playoff-worthy teams that need guards, and adding one of the NFL’s best at a time when they are rarely available is a reason to watch this. Swapping Nelson for Connor Colby would make the NFL’s best offense even more potent. It would mean zero weak links up front. The Colts played Seattle in Week 15 last year. I reference the Seahawks because Colby had one of the worst games in recent memory for any 49ers player a few weeks back on the road against Byron Murphy and Leonard Williams. Last December, Nelson had only one blown block against the run and a 0% pressure rate. Compare that to Colby’s 17.1% pressure rate allowed against Seattle in a game where he missed six blown blocks, one of the highest marks in the NFL this season. It’s a one-game comparison, but it gives you an idea of the kind of upgrade it’d be. Nelson’s consistency and floor make everyone around him better.

summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ injuries keep coming, and they keep winning anyway.
